title: Structural mechanism of substrate binding and inhibition of human taurine transporter

paper_content.abstract: Taurine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that plays several crucial roles in the body. Its uptake is mediated by the taurine transporter (TauT). Genetic mutations and dysregulation of TauT have been linked to various neurological disorders, cardiomyopathy, childhood progressive retinal degeneration, and cancer, making TauT a promising target for therapeutic intervention in these diseases. However, the structure and mechanism of TauT remain poorly understood. In this study, we present the structures of the human taurine transporter (hTauT) under four conditions: the substrate-free state, the taurine-bound state, the β-alanine-bound state, and the cyclic inhibitor piperidine-4-sulfonate (P4S)-bound state. These structures reveal that taurine binds at the central substrate-binding site of hTauT. Notably, β-alanine and the cyclic P4S inhibitors also mimic taurine, occupying the same substrate-binding site. In the substrate-free and P4S-bound forms, hTauT also adopt an inward-open conformation, where transmembrane helix TM1a bends toward the membrane, facilitating the opening of the intracellular gate for ion and substrate release. These structural insights enhance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying substrate and ion recognition and transport in hTauT, paving the way for the future development of taurine transporter substrate analogues or selective inhibitors.
paper_content.introduction:
Taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonic acid) is an abundant nonprotein β-amino acid and a conditionally essential nutrient widely distributed in most tissues of humans. Taurine has various physiological functions, including energy metabolism, osmoregulation, antioxidation, and neuromodulation 1. Taurine deficiency causes functional impairments in the central nervous system, cardiovascular system, immune response, skeletal muscle, and eye 1-5. The intracellular high levels of taurine are mainly regulated by the taurine transporters (TauT), which take taurine into cells 6. TauT-knockout mice exhibit aging characteristics, such as exercise intolerance and muscle atrophy, retinal and inner ear degeneration, renal development and function alteration, and cardiomyopathy 7,8. Mutations in the TauT genes are associated with neurological disorders, cardiomyopathy, and childhood progressive retinal degeneration in humans 9. In addition, TauT is overexpressed in several malignancies, such as colorectal (CRC), gastric (GC), and cervical cancers (CC), causing poor prognosis, immune evasion, aggressive and invasive progression, and recurrence of tumors 10-12. Therefore, TauT could be a promising diagnostic imaging and therapy target 13,14.

TauT (also known as SLC6A6) is a member of the solute carrier 6 (SLC6) family, which is divided into four subfamilies according to their substrate similarity—GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid), monoamine, neurotransmitter amino acid, and nutrient amino acid transporters. TauT shares >36% sequence similarity with other SLC6 family members, and has the highest sequence identity with GAT3 (~61%) 15. TauT, along with GAT1 (SLC6A1), GAT2 (SLC6A13), GAT3 (SLC6A11), BGT1 (SLC6A12), and CT1 (SLC6A8), belong to the GABA transporter subfamily 13. SLC6s can utilize the chemiosmotic gradient of sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl-) ions to transport their substrates across the membrane 15. For TauT, substrate uptake occurs with a stoichiometry of 2 Na⁺:1 Cl⁻. Today, the substrate taurine of TauT has been approved for treating congestive heart failure 1. Taurine also shows potential in acting as a therapeutic agent to treat muscle diseases 16, neurological disorders 17,18, cardiovascular diseases 19, metabolic diseases 18, and cancer 20. Inhibition of TauT could be a promising strategy in cancer treatment, yet only limited inhibitors that are structurally similar to substrate have been investigated. β-alanine is a linear inhibitor of TauT, previously identified as the substrate of TauT to take up with high efficiency in neuronal and astroglial cells 21,22. Piperidine-4-sulfonate (P4S) is a cyclic inhibitor of TauT developed with the amine group incorporated into the ring 23. P4S shows a relatively higher affinity than other investigated inhibitors and provides a potential lead structure to design specific drug candidates of TauT for therapy of cancer and neurodegenerative diseases 23.

Understanding how substrate binds to and is transported by TauT and inhibitors act on TauT are critical questions in the field of TauT. The taurine binding site on TauT was mapped based on the structure of Aquifex aeolicus LeuT, and mutations of several residues have been shown to significantly influence substrate recognition and uptake function of TauT 24. Moreover, homology modelling of TauT based on the related subfamily member GAT1 structure has provided valuable insights into the protein-ligand interactions 13. However, the structure of TauT remains unknown, precluding a thorough understanding of its transport mechanism and the structure-based development of medications.

Here, we show cryo-EM structures of human TauT (hTauT) in the apo, taurine-bound, β-alanine-bound, and P4S-bound states in the inward-occluded conformation at resolutions ranging from 2.7 to 2.9 Å, respectively. The apo state and the P4S-bound state also show inward-open conformations. These structures reveal the overall architecture, the linear substrate- and ion-binding sites, the conformational transition of hTauT, as well as the inhibitory mechanism of the cyclic P4S.
paper_content.results:
Structural determination and architecture of hTauT
Full-length wild-type human TauT (hTauT) was expressed with a green fluorescent protein (GFP) and maltose binding protein (MBP) at its N-terminus to monitor the behavior of hTauT protein via fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography (FSEC) 25,26 (Supplementary Fig. 1a). hTauT with the GFP-MBP tag showed good behavior and thermostability when solubilized in the n-dodecyl-β-d-maltoside (DDM) + cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) buffer (Supplementary Fig. 1a). A subsequent SEC-based thermal shift assay using purified proteins quantified this stabilization, showing the tagged hTauT had a melting temperature (Tm) of 82°C, significantly higher than the 46°C observed for untagged hTauT (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Therefore, full-length wild-type hTauT with the GFP-MBP tag was solubilized and purified in the DDM + CHS buffer with 150 mM NaCl throughout the solubilization and purification, owing to the essential roles of Na+ and Cl− ions in driving substrate uptake in SLC6s 15 (Supplementary Fig. 1b). The purified hTauT proteins were supplemented with different ligands for subsequent cryo-EM single-particle analyses (Supplementary Figs. 2-5). Initial single-particle processing of the apo and P4S-bound datasets indicated conformational heterogeneity, particularly in the TM1a helix, as evidenced by its discontinuous and poorly resolved density. This suggested significant flexibility, contrasting with the well-defined TM1a density observed in the stable, substrate-bound (taurine/β-alanine) states. To resolve this heterogeneity, we employed 3D variability analysis (3DVA) in cryoSPARC, which directly visualized the substantial flexibility of TM1a (Supplementary Movies 1-2). Subsequent focused 3D classification and refinement successfully separated two distinct conformations from these datasets: inward-occluded and inward-open (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 5). This strategy enabled us to determine high-resolution structures of hTauT in multiple conformational states: the apo state in the inward-occluded conformation and the inward-open conformation (2.8Å and 3.3 Å, respectively), the taurine-bound state in the inward-occluded conformation at 2.9 Å, the β-alanine-bound state in the inward-occluded conformation at 2.7 Å, and the P4S-bound state in the inward-occluded conformation and inward-open conformation (2.8 Å and 3.2 Å, respectively) (Supplementary Figs. 2-5 and Supplementary Table 1).

The qualities of these maps were all sufficient for model building of hTauT (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 1). hTauT adopts the canonical LeuT fold with 12 transmembrane helices (TM1-12), resolved with clear side chains (Fig. 1, and Supplementary Fig. 6). Among the 12 TMs of hTauT, TM1-TM5 and TM6-TM10, two structurally similar but topologically inverted repeats (IRs), form the transporter core (Fig. 1a), which resembles the canonical structure of other transporters in the SLC6 family 27,28. TM1 and TM6 are two broken short helices (TM1a-1b and TM6a-6b) (Fig. 1). TM11 and TM12 settle around the transporter core, and TM12 has a pronounced kink in the middle of the membrane (Fig. 1). Noticeably, in the taurine- and β-alanine-bound states, TM1a is highly stable with clear N-terminal densities from P39. For the apo and P4S-bound states, conformational flexibility of TM1a—initially evidenced by discontinuous density—was resolved through 3D variability analysis and focused 3D classification as described above, yielding four well-defined structures. Among these, TM1a is ordered from P39 in the P4S-bound inward-occluded, S45 in the P4S-bound inward-open, and E42 in the apo inward-open conformations. An exception is the apo inward-occluded structure, in which the N-terminal density for TM1a begins at residue F50 (Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 1).

The extracellular surface of hTauT is formed by the extracellular loops (EL2, EL3, EL4, and EL6) (Fig. 1a-b). Distinctly, the large EL2 (residues 154-217) has clear densities except for a small region (residues 180-189). A conserved disulfide bond formed between C162 and C171 stabilizes the base of EL2 (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 6). Both N/C terminuses of hTauT extend into the cytoplasm. 602–620 of the C-terminus were not resolved, probably due to the high flexibility of these regions (Supplementary Fig. 7). The intracellular surface is composed of the N/C terminuses and intracellular loops (IL3, IL4, and IL5) (Fig. 1a-b). The C terminus of hTauT (residues 568-620) is formed with two visible helices (designated CH1–2) (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Figs. 6 and 7), that have various interactions with IL1, IL3, and IL5 (Fig. 1b). This is in line with the important regulatory roles of the C terminus of hTauT in its surface expression and uptake activities 6,29.

The cryo-EM maps revealed several lipid-like densities surrounding the hTauT transmembrane domain (Fig. 1a, c-e). We identified that three densities occupy positions analogous to the previously characterized CHOL2 and CHOL3 sites in related SLC6 transporters 30, as well as an additional identified CHOL4 site in hDAT (Supplementary Fig. 8) 31. These three densities show the characteristic shape and size of sterols, which were modeled as cholesterol or CHS molecules (Supplementary Fig. 8). Notably, the conserved CHOL1 site, which stabilizes the outward conformation in other SLC6 transporters 30, was unoccupied in all our hTauT structures (Supplementary Fig. 8), consistent with our structures representing inward conformations.

Taurine-binding mechanism of hTauT
To measure the transporting activity of hTauT, we performed the substrate uptake assay using the LC/MS-MS method, as reported previously 32. The tagged hTauT exhibited taurine transport with a Km of 30.5 µM, comparable to the 24.8 µM measured for untagged hTauT (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 9a), and consistent with the previously reported value (Km = 37.3 µM) measured using the GFP-tagged hTauT in HEK293 cells 23. This confirmed that the fusion tag does not impair the transporter's fundamental function. To investigate the structural basis of taurine recognition by hTauT, we determined the structure of the hTauT-taurine complex at 2.9 Å (Supplementary Fig. 3). A strong density was observed at the substrate binding pocket in the taurine-bound state (Fig. 2b, c), while no visible density was observed in the apo state of hTauT, as no substrate was added during the apo sample preparation (Fig. 2c). The shape and size of the density match that of the taurine molecule, suggesting that this density represents the taurine substrate (Fig. 2c). The taurine coordinates into the substrate binding site of hTauT, surrounded by TM1, TM3, TM6, and TM8 (Fig. 2d), as that of SLC6 family members 32-34. The bound taurine is completely occluded from solvent access (Fig. 2b). Furthermore, the first turn of the intracellular side of TM5 is unwound at the conserved G(X9)P motif (G243(X9)P253 in hTauT), hydrating the Na2 site (Fig. 2b). These features are hallmarks of the inward-occluded conformation, as seen in other SLC6 transporters like hGAT1 35 and MhsT 36 (Supplementary Fig. 9b), confirming that taurine-bound hTauT is trapped in the inward-occluded conformation.

The substrate binding site of MATs is divided into the trilobed subsites (A, B, and C) 30. The subsite A of MATs is delimited by TM1b, TM6, and TM8 30. The sulfonic acid moiety of taurine deeply penetrates an enlarged subsite A of hTauT (denoted as a subsite AL), in which the relatively large negative aspartic acid on TM1b of MATs (D75 in hNET) is replaced by a small glycine (G60 in hTauT) (Supplementary Fig. 10c). This altered subsite organization, which has previously been observed in related transporters hGAT1 35 and rGAT1 32, creates a distinct binding architecture (Supplementary Fig. 10). Various interactions are formed between the sulfonic acid group of taurine and the expanded subsite AL of hTauT. The sulfonic acid group of taurine denotes multiple hydrogen bonds with the main chain amino groups of G60 and G62 on the flexible hinge region of TM1. Meanwhile, the sulfonic acid group forms several polar interactions with side chains of Y138 on TM6 and S402 on TM8 (Fig. 2d). Moreover, one oxygen atom of the sulfonic group of taurine coordinates Na at the Na1 site, which is further stabilized by chelating with N63 on TM1 (Fig. 2d). The hydrophobic ethane group of taurine protrudes into the subsite B lined by the hydrophobic residues L134 and Y138 on TM3, F300, A303, and L306 on TM6 (Fig. 2d). The terminal amino moiety of taurine establishes a salt bridge with the side chain of E406 on TM8 in subsite C and also forms hydrogen bonds with the main chain carboxylate group of F300 on TM6 and a water molecule (Fig. 2d). This is consistent with previous findings showing that G57E completely lost the activity, and F58I, L306Q, and E406C mutations reduced both the taurine uptake and binding affinity 24.

We next sought to understand the determinants of hTauT's specificity by comparing it with another taurine transporter, the proton-coupled amino acid transporter 1 (PAT1, SLC36A1). Sequence alignment and structural comparison with an AlphaFold3-predicted hPAT1 model reveal both common and distinct features (Supplementary Fig. 9c, d). Key small residues that form the enlarged subsite AL in hTauT (G57, G60, G62, S301) are completely conserved in hPAT1 (G59, G62, G64, S268), suggesting a shared mechanism for accommodating the taurine sulfonate group (Supplementary Fig. 9c, d). Furthermore, F300 and E406 in hTauT, which interact with the amino group, are conservatively replaced with F267 and Q350 in hPAT1 (Supplementary Fig. 9c, d). However, other critical residues are not conserved (Supplementary Fig. 9c, d). Most notably, F58—a unique determinant in hTauT that coordinates the Na1 site—is divergent in hPAT1 (Supplementary Fig. 9c, d). This difference likely contributes to hPAT1's broader substrate tolerance and its characteristically low affinity for taurine (Km > 1 mM), contrasting with the high-affinity, selective transport by hTauT 37.

A comparative analysis across the SLC6 family reveals how the conserved LeuT fold has been evolutionarily adapted. The substrate binding modes were compared among taurine to hTauT, GABA to hGAT1 (PDB: 7Y7W, GABA transporter subfamily) 35, glycine to hGlyT1 (PDB: 8WFI, neurotransmitter amino acid transporter subfamily) 38, and noradrenaline to hNET (PDB: 8ZPB, MAT subfamily) 39 in their occluded conformations (Supplementary Fig. 10). Noticeably, the binding mode of taurine to hTauT closely resembles that of GABA to hGAT1 (Cα RMSD of 1.627 Å) and glycine to hGlyT1 (Cα RMSD of 2.535 Å) (Supplementary Fig. 10a, b). A key distinction, however, is that the taurine sulfonate group (with three oxygen atoms) engages in a more extensive hydrogen-bonding network than the carboxylate groups (with two oxygen atoms) of GABA or glycine. Moreover, several unique residues in hTauT (G57, F58, E406) are substituted in hGAT1 (Y60, A61, T400), explaining their distinct substrate profiles and the low affinity of hTauT for GABA 40. In contrast, hMATs like hNET have evolved a fundamentally different binding site configuration 41. The electronegative catechol moieties of monoamines are profoundly extended into the enlarged subsite B lined by the glycine on TM1b (E406 in hTauT), while their electropositive amino groups are anchored in a smaller subsite A by the large acidic residues (D75 in hNET), instead (Supplementary Fig. 10c). This configuration is inverse to that of hTauT, which features a small glycine (G60) in subsite AL and a large, acidic residue (E406) in subsite C (Supplementary Fig. 10c). This comparison underscores the remarkable versatility of the SLC6 scaffold, which has been tailored through specific residue changes to transport chemically diverse substrates.

The binding of substrate β-alanine to hTauT
TauT was originally identified as a taurine/β-alanine transporter, which can transport both taurine and β-alanine and similar Km values were measured using HEK293 cells (37.3 and 44.5 μM for taurine and β-alanine, respectively) 23. We confirmed that β-alanine acts as a competitive inhibitor of taurine uptake, with a Ki of 55.0 µM (Fig. 3a). To explore the binding mode of β-alanine, we resolved the structure of β-alanine-bound hTauT at 2.7 Å (Supplementary Fig. 4). Further inspection of the cryo-EM map revealed an isolated and prominent density at the substrate binding site, which aligns well with the structure of the β-alanine molecule (Fig. 3b, c). The binding pocket is blocked from both the extra- and intracellular sides and the intracellular side of TM5 is unwound, indicating that the β-alanine-hTauT complex also adopts an inward-occluded conformation (Fig. 3b). Similar to taurine, β-alanine also has a basic amine group and an acidic moiety connected by a linear two-carbon linker. The acidic moiety of β-alanine is a carboxy group instead of the sulfonic group in taurine. Two oxygen atoms of the carboxy group are also penetrated into the extended subsite AL and form multiple hydrogen bonds with residues with hTauT (Fig. 3d). One oxygen atom coordinates with Na+ at the Na1 site to bridge the interaction with F58 and N63 on TM1, and S301 on TM6. The other oxygen forms hydrogen bonds with the main chain amino group of G62 on TM1 and the side chain hydroxyl group of Y138 on TM3 (Fig. 3d). Additionally, the ethane group linker and the amino group of β-alanine form the same interaction as that of taurine with hTauT: the two-carbon linker is nested into the subsites C lined by the hydrophobic side chain of L134 and Y138 on TM2, F300, A303, and L306 on TM6, and the amino group of β-alanine also forms a hydrogen bond with the side chain of E406 on TM8 and water-mediated interactions with the main chain carboxylate group of F300 on TM6 and the side chain of Q403 on TM8 (Fig. 3d). Therefore, the interactions of β-alanine with hTauT are almost the same as those of taurine with hTauT; only the hydrogen bond network of the carboxy group of β-alanine with hTauT is less than that of taurine with hTauT, which has three oxygen atoms from the sulfonic group (Fig. 3e). This is in agreement with the functional analysis that hTauT has a higher affinity to taurine than β-alanine 42.

The binding of cyclic inhibitor P4S to hTauT
Different from β-alanine, P4S is a cyclic substrate analog of taurine containing one acidic and one amino head group linked by carbon chains 23. P4S acts as a competitive inhibitor of taurine transport by hTauT 23 and can dose-dependently inhibit the taurine uptake of hTauT with a Ki of 1.5 mM (Fig. 4a). To elucidate the binding mode of P4S with hTauT, we determined the P4S-bound hTauT complex structure in the inward-occluded conformation at 2.8 Å resolution (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 5). A distinct P4S density was observed at the substrate-binding pocket of hTauT (Fig. 4c). Similarly, the sulfonic acid group of P4S protrudes into subsite AL and forms multiple hydrogen bonds with the main-chain amino group of G60 and G62 on TM1a, the side-chain hydroxyl oxygen of Y138 on TM3, and S402 on TM8 (Fig. 4d). Furthermore, one oxygen atom of the sulfonic group of P4S coordinates Na+ at the Na1 site, identically to that of taurine (Fig. 4d). However, the rigid piperidine ring of P4S forms a boat conformation to fit less optimally into the hydrophobic subsite C of the substrate binding site. The piperidine ring confers relative rigidity to the nitrogen group, in which the interaction of nitrogen with E406 is disrupted (Fig. 4e). This is in agreement with the fact that the P4S is not a high-affinity inhibitor of hTauT with a high Ki. To validate the functional role of these residues at the P4S binding site, we designed a series of mutations (Fig. 4f). Surface expression assays revealed that most mutants were properly trafficked, with the exception of G62Y, which showed reduced expression (Supplementary Fig. 11a). As most residues in the P4S-binding site are also involved in substrate binding, mutagenesis of key binding site residues abolished uptake activity (Fig. 4f). Notably, the E406G mutation, which disrupts a critical salt bridge for taurine binding, resulted in a complete loss of function, underscoring its essential role (Fig. 4f).

Interestingly, besides the inward-occluded conformation, we also captured hTauT in an inward-open conformation in the presence of P4S at 3.2 Å resolution (Figs. 1, 5a, Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 1). The P4S-bound inward-open structure is highly similar to the apo inward-open structure with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 0.576 over 540 aligned Cα atoms (Supplementary Fig. 11b). In both the P4S-bound or apo inward-open structure, a pronounced bend of TM1a towards the membrane plane, coupled with unwinding of the intracellular side of TM5, collectively open a solvent-accessible pathway to the cytoplasm (Fig. 5b, Supplementary Fig. 11b). These structural features are consistent with the inward-open conformation of related transporters hGAT1, hGAT3, and hGlyT1, but distinct from the outward-tilted TM5 helix observed in the inward-open LeuT (Supplementary Fig. 11c) 35,43-45. In the substrate-binding site, there is a clear, well-defined density in the P4S-bound state, but does not exist in the inward-open conformation of the apo state (Fig. 5b). The density is sufficient to assign the P4S molecule. The P4S’s configuration is nearly identical between the inward-occluded and inward-open conformations (Fig. 5c). In the inward-open conformation, the sulfonic acid group of P4S remains engaged with subsite AL of hTauT and forms four hydrogen bonds with the main-chain amino group of G62 on TMl, the side-chain hydroxyl oxygen of Y138 on TM3, S301 on TM6 and S402 on TM8 (Fig. 5c). The principal conformational changes are the ~54° outward splaying of TM1a and further unwinding of the intracellular side of TM5 in the inward-open conformation (Fig. 5d). The movement of TM1a directly severs the hydrogen bond between P4S and G60 on TM1a. Furthermore, it disrupts the Na1 site, abolishing the Na⁺-mediated interactions with F58 and N63 on TM1a (Fig. 5c, d). Thus, while P4S remains bound in the inward-open conformation, its interactions with the transporter are partially destabilized due to the displacement of TM1a. This mechanism, wherein a substrate or substrate analog is retained in a partially weakened state during the gating transition, mirrors observations from noradrenaline-bound hNET structures 39. A comparison of substrate-binding modes in the inward-open conformation further highlights the divergent strategies employed by SLC6 subfamilies. Consistent with our analysis of the inward-occluded conformation, the binding architecture of hTauT is inverted relative to monoamine transporters. In the inward-open hNET, the electronegative catechol moiety of noradrenaline penetrates an enlarged subsite B, while its electropositive amino group is anchored in subsite A by a large acidic residue (D75). In stark contrast, hTauT employs a small glycine (G60) in subsite AL to accommodate the sulfonate group and a large acidic residue (E406) in subsite C to coordinate the amino group (Supplementary Fig. 11d). This conserved, inverted binding motif underscores a fundamental structural determinant of substrate specificity that is maintained throughout the transport cycle.

Conformational equilibrium of apo and P4S-bound hTauT
Following 3DVA and focused 3D classification, we resolved two distinct inward conformations of apo hTauT (Fig. 1a, b). The inward-occluded conformation, reconstructed from 149,606 particles, features an occluded substrate-binding site and a partially unwound intracellular segment of TM5 (Supplementary Fig. 12a). This conformation is nearly identical to the taurine-bound inward-occluded state, with a RMSD of 1.250 Å over 542 aligned Cα atoms (Supplementary Fig. 12b). In contrast, the inward-open conformation, determined from 80,335 particles (~35%), is virtually superimposable with the P4S-bound inward-open structure (RMSD 0.576 Å; Supplementary Fig. 11b). A comparison between the two apo conformations reveals that the transition to the inward-open conformation is characterized by a ~62° outward splaying of TM1a and further unwinding of the intracellular side of TM5, which opens a cytoplasmic pathway (Fig. 6a). The particle distribution (~65% inward-occluded vs. ~35% inward-open) in the apo state indicates a dynamic equilibrium with a preference for the inward-occluded conformation. The coexistence of both conformations suggests the apo transporter samples a dynamic conformational ensemble, which likely includes outward conformations. We therefore propose that apo hTauT exists in a dynamic equilibrium; when it transiently visits an outward-open conformation, taurine binding primes the transporter for translocation. This intrinsic conformational plasticity is a shared feature among SLC6 transporters, such as GlyT1 and SERT 44,46.

Strikingly, P4S binding reinforces this equilibrium. In the P4S-bound state, the majority of particles (~80%) populate the inward-occluded conformation, with a minority (~20%) in the inward-open state. This pronounced population shift demonstrates that P4S binding preferably stabilizes the inward-occluded conformation, which is structurally rationalized by the enhanced ligand-protein interactions observed in this state (Fig. 5d).

Structural change of hTauT from the occluded conformation to the inward conformation
To reveal how hTauT transits from the inward-occluded conformation to the inward-open conformation to release the taurine substrate into the cytosol, we next compare the taurine-bound hTauT structure (inward-occluded) with the apo hTauT structure (inward-open conformation). The structure of hTauT-apo can be superimposed to that of taurine-hTauT with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) value of 3.321 Å over 543 aligned Cα atoms (Fig. 6b). Most of the structures between these two conformations are the same except TM1a and further unwound TM5, which will be discussed later (Fig. 6b). Above the substrate binding site of both the inward-occluded and inward-open conformations, various interactions are formed among residues from the tightly packed TM1b, TM3, TM6a, and TM10 to close the extracellular pathway (Fig. 6c). F300 on TM6a interacts with Y138 on TM3, and R66 on TM1a forms a salt bridge with D459 on TM10 (Fig. 6c), which are two highly conserved EC-gate pairs in the SLC6 family for the closure of the EC gate 30. In addition, R66 forms a cation-π interaction with F300 and a hydrogen bonding network with the surrounding residues L61, L70, Q297, D459 and S464 to stabilize the closed EC-gate (Fig. 6c). R66 contributes two hydrogen bonds to D459 and one to Q297 and S464, respectively. The extensive interactions observed alongside the extracellular vestibule of hTauT are reminiscent of the inward-occluded structures of GAT135. A notable conformational change is TM1a between these two conformations (Fig. 6b). TM1a of the inward-open conformation unwinds the last helical turn (56-GGFVG-60) and bends approximately 53° towards the membrane (Fig. 6b), resulting in an open pathway from the central pocket to the cytoplasm. Below the substrate binding site of the inward-occluded conformation, the TM1a occludes the permeation pathway of the substrate to the cytosol. The main chain of G57 on TM1a forms a hydrogen bond with S402 on TM8, while G57 in TM1a of the inward-open conformation swing away from the central pocket, resulting in an open pathway from the central pocket to the cytoplasm (Fig. 6d). Various interactions lead to a tightly packed substrate pocket with a relatively stable TM1a in the inward-occluded conformation of the taurine/β-alanine-bound states. Three IC gate pairs are formed to stabilize the inward-occluded conformation further (Fig. 6d), which are conserved in the SLC6 family 30. W44 on TM1a forms a π-π stacking with Y315 on TM6. Two salt bridges are formed between R41 on TM1a and D416 on TM8 and K47 on TM1a and D325 on TM7, respectively (Fig. 6d). Meanwhile, R41 forms a hydrogen bond with Y315 on TM6.

hTauT plays an important role in osmoregulation to control cell volume; the Na+/Cl− gradient is utilized to determine taurine intake 6. Our high-quality cryo-EM maps enabled us to identify the binding sites of these ions. In the inward-occluded taurine-hTauT structure, Na1 is coordinated by the sulfonic oxygen of taurine, the carbonyl oxygen of F58 on TM1, S301 on TM6a, the side-chain carbonyl oxygen of N63 on TM1b, and the amide of N333 on TM7 (Fig. 6e), and the Na2 site is coordinated by the main-chain carbonyls of G56 and V59 on TM1 and L398 on TM8, as well as the side-chain oxygens of D401 and S402 on TM8 (Fig. 6f). The Cl− site is coordinated by the side-chain hydroxyls of Y83 on TM1, S301 on TM6a, and S337 on TM7, as well as the side-chain amides of Q297 on TM6a in both the inward-occluded conformation of taurine-bound state and inward-open conformation of P4S-bound state (Fig. 6g, Supplementary Fig. 11e). However, in the central substrate-binding pocket of the inward-open conformation of the apo state, the densities at the Na1, Na2 and Cl- sites were all absent (Fig. 6e, f, g). Compared with the inward-occluded state, the local structural organization of the Na1 and Na2 sites in the inward-open state has notably changed owing to the conformational change of TM1a. The carbonyl groups of G56, F58 and V59 on TM1a swing away from the Na1 and Na2 sites, respectively (Fig. 6e, f), resulting in the disrupted sodium-binding sites. Integrating these findings with previous studies demonstrates that the inward-occluded SLC6 transporters chelate the Na+ and Cl- ions for substrate binding; in contrast, inward-open SLC6s have disrupted Na1 and Na2 sites, facilitating the release of sodium and substrate into the cytosol 35,47. The absent density for Cl- in the inward-open apo state probably owing to its lower resolution or chloride release in this state.

Our structural data demonstrate that P4S can bind to both the inward-occluded and inward-open conformations of hTauT, analogous to how noradrenaline binds to multiple conformations of hNET33. This multi-state binding, its structural analogy to taurine, and its known role as a competitive inhibitor suggested it might itself be a transported substrate. To test this hypothesis, we performed a decisive efflux assay 48,49. P4S induced the efflux of preloaded [3H]taurine from HEK293-hTauT cells. Crucially, pretreatment with monensin (which elevates intracellular [Na+]) significantly augmented P4S-induced efflux (Fig. 7a). This potentiation is a key functional characteristic consistent with SLC6 substrate translocation, as it indicates a Na⁺-coupled exchange process, rather than the action of a simple, static inhibitor. In order to further elucidate whether P4S could be transported as a substrate or acts as an orthosteric inhibitor, we sought to compare the structure of the P4S-bound hTauT with the structures in other conformations with the full transport cycle. Because the outward conformation structure of hTauT was not available, we utilized the structures of the PF-03463275-bound hGlyT1 (outward-open conformation) 38 as a substitute. hTauT and hGlyT1 share high sequence similarity and similar occluded and inward-open conformations (Supplementary Fig. 7) and are likely to own a similar outward conformation. We aligned these structures based on the motifs near their substrate binding site (Supplementary Fig. 12c). From the inward-occluded conformation to the outward-open conformation, TM1b and TM6a move away from taurine/β-alanine and P4S (Supplementary Fig. 12c), while from the inward-occluded conformation to the inward-open conformation, TM1a moves away from both P4S and the physiological substrates taurine/β-alanine (Supplementary Fig. 12d). Therefore, the structures in the different conformations during the transport cycle are fully compatible with the binding of P4S, the same as that of taurine/β-alanine (Fig. 7b). Therefore, collectively, the functional efflux data and structural analysis provide conclusive evidence that P4S is not merely an orthosteric inhibitor but a translocatable substrate analog that competes with taurine for binding and undergoes the full Na⁺-coupled transport cycle.
paper_content.methods:
Cell culture
HEK293F suspension cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were cultured in FreeStyle 293 medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 1% FBS at 37 °C with an atmosphere of 5% CO2 and 70% humidity. HEK293T adherent cells (ATCC) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS at 37 °C with 5% CO2. Expi 293F suspension cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were cultured in 293F Hi-exp medium (Shanghai OPM Biosciences). Sf9 insect cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were grown in SIM SF medium (Sino Biological) at 27 °C.

Expression constructs and detergents screening
The complementary DNA (cDNA) of human TauT (1–620; UniProt: P31641) was purchased from HedgehogBio Science and Technology Ltd. (catalog number: HH-gene-1116). The cDNA of hTauT contains nine epitope transfer mutations (F58A, L306Q, E406G, G62Y, G60Y, L61A, L134A, S301A, G57A) were cloned into a modified BacMam expression vector 51 with the N-terminal GFP-MBP tag. GFP is fused with two strep tags in its loop for affinity purification. All primer sequences are provided in the Source Data file. The BacMam plasmids containing the gene of hTauT were small-scale transient transfected into HEK293F cells. The cells were collected after 48 h transfection and solubilized in different detergents to screen detergents and stability of hTauT via fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography (FSEC) on the Superose 6 increase 5/150 GL column (Cytiva). Detergents were used at the following concentrations: 1% (w/v) DDM plus 0.1% (w/v) CHS, 1% (w/v) DDM, 1% (w/v) lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (MNG), 1% (w/v) MNG plus 0.1% (w/v) CHS, 1% digitonin, and 1% (w/v) glyco-diosgenin (GDN).

Protein expression and purification
The baculoviruses of hTauT were produced with the Bac-to-Bac system and amplified in Sf9 insect cells. HEK293F cells were typically infected with a 7% (v/v) volume of infection of the P2 virus at a density of 2.5-3.0 × 106 ml−1. 10 mM sodium butyrate was added to the culture 8-12 h post-infection. Cells were collected 48 h post-infection by centrifugation at 3,500 g for 10 min and washed once with 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0 and 150 mM NaCl. The harvested cells were then flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C. The protein was extracted from cells by resuspending the pellet with 20 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2 µg ml−1 aprotinin, 2 µg ml−1 pepstatin, 2 µg ml−1 leupeptin, 1 mM phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), and solubilized with 1% (w/v) n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside (DDM; Anatrace) and 0.1% (w/v) cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS; Anatrace) at 4 °C for 1 h. The insolubilized cell debris was removed by centrifugation at 3,500 g for 15 min. The supernatant was obtained by ultracentrifugation at 100,000 g for 1 h and then loaded onto 5 ml of Streptactin Beads 4FF (Smart-Lifesciences). Wash buffer containing 20 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 0.025% DDM, and 0.0025% CHS was used to remove contaminating proteins. The target protein was eluted with 20 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 0.025% DDM, 0.0025% CHS, and 2.5 mM desthiobiotin (IBA Lifesciences). After adding 1 mM DTT, 10 mM MgCl2 and 2 mM ATP to remove contamination of heat shock proteins, the eluted target protein was concentrated with a 50 kDa cut-off concentrator (Millipore) and further purified by the Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) running in a buffer containing 20 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 0.025% DDM, and 0.0025% CHS. The peak fractions related to the target protein on SDS-PAGE and showing good properties on native-PAGE were combined and concentrated for cryo-EM sample preparation.

Thermal stability assay
Thermal stability assays were performed according to a previously established protocol 25 with modification. Tagged and untagged hTauT proteins (1 µg and 2 µg, respectively) were diluted in assay buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 0.025% (w/v) DDM, 0.0025% (w/v) CHS) to a final volume of 100 µL. The solutions were heated for 15 minutes at specified temperatures in a thermal cycler. Denatured protein was subsequently removed by ultracentrifugation at 98,400 × g for 20 minutes using a Type 42.2Ti rotor (Beckman Coulter). The resulting supernatants were analyzed by FSEC. The FSEC peak heights for hTauT were normalized to the value from an unheated control sample. Melting temperatures (Tm) were determined by fitting the normalized data to a sigmoidal dose-response model in GraphPad Prism 8.

Uptake assay
HEK293T cells were first seeded into a 6-well plate at a density of 2.0 × 106 cells per well and infected with 0.5% (v/v) P2 virus after culturing for 12 h. 24 h-post infection, HEK293T cells were trypsinized for 1 min and seeded into a poly-d-lysine-treated 96-well plate at 2.0 × 106 cells per well in 100 μL culture medium. The supernatant of the 96-well plate was discarded 36 h after infection, and the cells were washed three times with uptake buffer consisting of 119 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM CaCl₂, 1.2 mM MgSO₄, 1.2 mM KH₂PO₄, 4.7 mM KCl, 11 mM glucose, and 25 mM HEPES in distilled water, adjusted to pH 7.4 using NaOH. Saturation experiments were conducted with seven concentrations of taurine-d4 ranging from 0.4 μM to 640 μM. For competition experiments, β-alanine ranging from 1 μM to 10 mM and P4S ranging from 10 μM to 100 μM were pre-incubated at 37 °C for 4 min and 15 min, respectively. Then, 5 µM taurine-d4 was co-incubated with the same concentration ranges of β-alanine and P4S for 1 min at 37 °C. The stated concentrations always refer to the final assay volume of 100 μL. Uptake was terminated by washing the plates three times with cold PBS buffer. Cells were lysed at 4°C for 2 h by adding 100 μL of lysis buffer per well, which consisted of 90% methanol and 10% distilled water (v/v), containing 1 μM taurine-13C2 as an internal standard. Plates were subjected to LC-MS/MS quantification of taurine-d4. Nonspecific uptake was determined analogously with HEK293T cells infected with 0.05% (v/v) P2 virus of empty vector. Transport kinetics were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 8 software by fitting substrate concentration–uptake rate response curves. In the saturation experiment, specific uptake was calculated as the difference between total and nonspecific uptake. Saturation curves were generated using nonlinear regression analysis with the equation y = Vmax × x / (Km + x). Values of both IC50 and Ki were obtained by data interpolation of % Inhibition and the equation IC50 = Ki (1 + [S] / Km), respectively.

The chromatographic separation was performed on a Thermo Vanquish liquid chromatograph (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with an OSAKA SODA CAPCELL PAK ADME column (2.1 mm × 100 mm, 3 μm) maintained at 35 °C. The mobile phases were water (A) and acetonitrile (B), both containing 0.1% formic acid at a flow rate of 0.2 mL min-1. The elution procedure was set as follows: 0-1.5 min, 2% B; 1.6-3.8 min, 85% B; 3.9-8.0 min, 2% B. The autosampler was kept at 15 °C. Mass spectrometry was carried out on a Q Exactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The capillary temperature was set to 320 °C, and the spray voltage was +3,500 V. Positive ion analysis was carried out in the selected-ion-monitoring mode. The resolution, maximum IT, and AGC target values were set at 70,000, 100 ms, and 3e6. The monitoring ions were 130.04705 and 128.02866 for taurine-d4 and taurine-13C2, respectively. The raw data was acquired using Xcalibur 4.1.31.9 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Cell surface biotinylation and immunoblot analysis
Cell surface biotinylation was conducted as described before 52 with modification. HEK293T cells were seeded in six-well plates at a density of 2.0 × 10⁶ cells per well and subsequently infected with baculovirus for the expression of untagged hTauT, GFP-MBP-tagged hTauT, or its mutants. The titer of the P2 virus for each sample was standardized based on total protein expression levels measured by FSEC. At 36 hours post-infection, cells were washed three times with ice-cold PBS (pH 8.0). Subsequently, 500 µL of 1.5 mM Sulfo-NHS-LC-biotin (APExBIO) in PBS (pH 8.0) was added to each well, and the plates were incubated at room temperature for 1 hour. The reaction was quenched by replacing the biotin solution with ice-cold 10 mM glycine in TBS (pH 8.0). After washing with TBS (pH 8.0), cells were lysed with 1% DDM in TBS (pH 8.0) for 40 min on ice, followed by centrifugation at 16,125 × g for 20 minutes. The supernatants were incubated with HRV-3C protease for 15 minutes at 4°C to cleave the GFP-MBP tag. The lysates were then incubated with Streptactin Beads 4FF (Smart-Lifesciences) for 2 hours at 4°C. The beads were collected by centrifugation at 1,000 × g, and the flow-through was discarded. After four washes with lysis buffer, bound proteins were eluted with elution buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 3 mM biotin, 100 mM DDT, 2% SDS) for 7 minutes at room temperature. The eluates were treated with PNGase F in Glycoprotein Denaturing Buffer (400 mM DTT, 5% SDS, 10% NP-40 in TBS, pH 8.0) at 37°C for 1 hour and then separated on a 12% gradient SDS-PAGE gel. For immunoblot analysis, proteins were transferred to a membrane and probed with an anti-Na+/K+ ATPase antibody (1:20,000; Abcam; ab76020) followed by goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (1:5,000; Lablead; S0101) as a loading control to normalize sample volumes. hTauT was detected using an anti-hTauT antibody (1:1,000; Santa Cruz; sc-393036) followed by goat anti-mouse secondary antibody (1:5,000; Lablead; S0100).

Radiolabelled taurine release assay
Release assay was performed as previously described 48 with modification. Expi293F cells were infected with 0.5% (v/v) P2 virus of hTauT and incubated for 24 h to reach a density of 3.0 × 10⁶ cells. The culture medium was removed, and cells were loaded with 10 nM [³H]taurine in Krebs-Ringer-HEPES buffer (KHB: 120 mM NaCl, 3 mM KCl, 2 mM CaCl₂, 2 mM MgCl₂, 20 mM glucose, 10 mM HEPES, pH 7.3) for 20 minutes at 37°C. The cells were then equilibrated to room temperature and washed five times with KHB. Following a 10-minute pre-incubation in either KHB alone or KHB containing 10 µM monensin, the supernatant was discarded. The release protocol was initiated with four sequential 2-minute incubations in 100 µL of the corresponding buffer (KHB or KHB + monensin), with supernatant collection at each interval. Test compounds, dissolved in the same buffers, were then applied for five additional 2-minute cycles. Taurine (400 µM) was used as a positive control. Each condition was tested in duplicate across three independent experiments. Collected supernatants were mixed with a liquid scintillation cocktail, and radioactivity was quantified by scintillation counting.

Cryo-EM sample preparation and data acquisition
The purified wild-type hTauT protein was concentrated to about A280=20 (11 mg ml⁻¹) to prepare the apo samples and incubated at 4°C for 2 h with 2 mM taurine, 5 mM β-alanine, or 2 mM P4S separately to prepare substrate-bound samples and inhibitor-bound samples. Then, 2.5 µL of the sample was added to holey carbon grids (GIG-Cu 300 mesh, R 1/1) glow-discharged for 2 min using 25% O2 and 75% Ar by the Solarus advanced plasma system (Gatan). The sampled grids were blotted for 4 s with a blot force of 2 after a 5 s incubation on the grids at 4 °C under 100% humidity and then plunge-frozen in liquid ethane cooled by liquid nitrogen using a Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

A Talos Arctica electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operating at 200 kV and equipped with a K2 camera (Gatan) was first used to screen the quality of samples on cryo-EM grids. Cryo-EM data were acquired on a 300 kV Titan Krios electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a K3 Summit direct electron detector (Gatan) mounted after a quantum energy filter set to a slit width of 20 eV.

For taurine-bound hTauT, movie stacks were collected using EPU software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in super-resolution mode at a magnification of ×64,000 with a pixel size of 0.54 Å and a defocus range of -1.5 to -1.8 µm. Each movie stack consisting of 32 frames was exposed for 2.68 s, yielding a total dose of about 50 e- Å-2 with a dose rate of 21.8 e- pixel-1 s-1. For the apo state, β-alanine- and P4S-bound hTauT, movie stacks were obtained using EPU software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in super-resolution mode at a magnification of ×81,000 with a calibrated pixel size of 0.5335 Å and a defocus range of -1.5 µm to -1.8 µm. Each movie stack consisting of 32 frames was exposed for 2.56 s, yielding a total dose of about 50 e- Å-2 with a dose rate of 22.36 e- pixel-1 s-1.

Cryo-EM data processing
The data-processing workflows are displayed in Supplementary Figs. 2-5 and Supplementary Table 1. A total of 1,216 multi-frame movies of taurine-bound hTauT were collected. The beam-induced motion was corrected and twofold binned to a pixel size of 1.08 Å with dose weighting applied using MotionCor2 53. After manually removing empty carbon and micrographs with ice or ethane contamination, the dose-weighted micrographs were then imported into cryoSPARC 54, and contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters were estimated using patch-CTF estimation 55. Blob picker was used for initial particle selection from 1,210 out of a total of 1,216 micrographs, followed by several rounds of 2D classification, resulting in the selection of 269,729 particles to generate a good initial model with obvious secondary structure features by ab initio reconstruction. With the help of the good model, particles from a total of 1,210 micrographs were re-picked using Topaz 56, and seed-facilitated 3D classification 57 was performed to improve resolution. After seed-facilitated 3D classification and multi-reference 3D classification, the final map reached a resolution of 2.9 Å using non-uniform refinement 58 followed by local refinement with the soft mask covering hTauT.

For the apo state, β-alanine- and P4S-bound hTauT datasets, 2,628, 1,008, and 6,381 super-resolution movie stacks were collected, corrected, and twofold binned to a pixel size of 1.067 Å with dose weighting applied using MotionCor2, and micrographs showing contamination and empty carbon were manually excluded. The dose-weighted micrographs were then imported into cryoSPARC, and CTF parameters were estimated using patch-CTF estimation.

After being picked by the blob picker, 1,820,272 particles of β-alanine-bound hTauT were selected for two rounds of 2D classification to generate a good initial model with obvious secondary structure features by ab initio reconstruction. Seed-facilitated 3D classification and multi-reference 3D classification were performed to further improve the resolution to 3.7 Å. Particles were re-picked using two rounds of Topaz, processed for seed-facilitated 3D classification and multi-reference 3D classification to improve the map quality. Non-uniform refinement followed by local refinement with the soft mask covering hTauT was used to obtain final maps with resolutions of 2.7 Å for the β-alanine-bound hTauT.

Particles of the apo and P4S-bound states were picked by the blob picker underwent several seed-facilitated 3D classifications and multi-reference 3D classifications using the good reference to obtain a good initial model with a resolution of 3.6 Å for the apo state and 3.7 Å for the P4S-bound hTauT generated by its own particles. Particles were re-picked using Topaz, processed for seed-facilitated 3D classification and multi-reference 3D classification to improve the map quality. Further processing of the apo and P4S-bound datasets still showed discontinuous and poorly resolved density of TM1a, which indicates conformational heterogeneity. To resolve this heterogeneity, we employed 3D variability analysis (3DVA) in cryoSPARC. A consensus refinement map, low-pass filtered to 6 Å, served as the initial reference. A soft mask was applied to focus the analysis on the dynamic TM1a region. The 3DVA was computed for 3 modes over a maximum of 20 iterations. Following this, particles were visualized and sorted using the 3DVA display tool with a windowing setting of 2, which organized them into 20 overlapping classes based on their position along the computed mode. This analysis directly visualized the substantial flexibility of TM1a (Supplementary Movies 1-2). Subsequent 3DVA and focused 3D classification successfully resolved this heterogeneity, distinguishing two distinct conformational states (the inward-open and inward-occluded conformations) for both the apo and P4S-bound hTauT. To further improve map quality, a second round of particle picking was performed with Topaz. The resulting particles were subjected to seed-facilitated and multi-reference 3D classification. For the inward-occluded conformation of both the apo and P4S-bound hTauT, non-uniform refinement followed by local refinement with the soft mask covering hTauT was used to obtain final maps with resolutions of 2.8 Å. To specifically improve the density for the dynamic TM1a region in the inward-open states, we applied focused 3D classification centered on this helix, followed by non-uniform and local refinement. This strategy yielded final maps at 3.3 Å for the inward-open conformations of the apo state and 3.2 Å for the P4S-bound hTauT.

Model building and refinement
The initial structure model of hTauT was computationally generated using AlphaFold3 (AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, #AF-P31641-F1) 59 and then fitted into the cryo-EM map using UCSF Chimera X 60 and rebuilt manually using Coot 61. Phenix.real_space_refine and phenix.validation_cryoem tools in PHENIX 62 were used to further refine and validate models to obtain final structures. The model-related metrics, including MolProbity scores, clash scores, rotamer outliers, and statistics of the Ramachandran plots, were summarized in Supplementary Table 1. Figures were displayed with PyMOL63 and ChimeraX. The sigma levels for all presented density figures were calculated in ChimeraX through division of the threshold level by the standard deviation (SD).

Quantification and statistical analysis
Global resolution estimations of cryo-EM density maps are based on the 0.143 Fourier shell correlation criterion. The local resolution was estimated using cryoSPARC. The figure legends detail the number of technical replicates (n), along with relevant statistical parameters for each experiment. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. The cell lines were routinely checked to be negative for mycoplasma contamination but have not been authenticated.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The manuscript by Qi, Zhang, and colleagues present human taurine transporter (TauT) structures in different states, revealing how taurine, β-alanine, and a putative inhibitor cyclic P4S bind to the substrate-binding site. The authors’ findings provide key insights into TauT’s transport mechanism, aiding future drug development. The manuscript is well and clearly written and provides a wealth of data - mostly derived from cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) approaches. While the structural work is at a very high standard – it does not come along with biochemical controls as it would be required to support the findings. Just a few things that the authors may take into consideration exploring: 1) The authors use an N-terminal GFP-MBP tag to use this construct expressed in HEK293 cells in suspension; however, it has not been described whether the construct is fully functional. The uptake assay performed in Figure 2, panel A, does not give the details of whether this particular construct has been used (and there is a typo: wide-type instead of wild type hTauT). Maybe the authors have performed these experiments and published the findings in an earlier paper – then, they ought to simply cite the evidence. If not, they must present the functionality of TauT in this specific vector by an uptake assay since the assay is anyway already up and running. 2) The number of structures in occluded or inward-open conformation is impressive and the authors have made a very good job in deciphering all these. However, since structural biological answers aided by cryo-EM largely relies on assumptions and interpretations of data, it would be helpful if the authors would add data of mutagenesis experiments. The manuscript includes quite a number of very plausible amino acid contact points with substrates or inhibitors; hence, it would be an easy task to mutate some key residues to ascertain loss of function and thereby support the findings of the cryo-EM approach (I am especially focusing on Figure 4 for this request). 3) The question whether cyclic P4S is a substrate or inhibitor cannot be answered by the assay the group has used in this manuscript. This ought to be done in a trans-acceleration experiment or also by a release assay: here. tritiated taurine is being transported into the TauT-expressing cells, and then, unlabeled taurine or unlabeled P4S is being used in increasing concentrations. In case of taurine, the tritiated taurine will be released by the transporter upon the inward-transport by the taurine applied from the outside. However, the problem is that the efflux can be elevated but still not be decisively showing that the compound is a substrate because in some instances, pseudo-efflux may take place. Since TauT is a member of the SLC6-family and related to GABA-transporter, it is dependent on sodium. To determine the substrate status of P4S, the authors should use monensin, a sodium-proton ionophor, which will selectively elevate sodium ions intracellularly while depleting protons. This activity will then be decisive to unravel the substrate status of the compound: Only substrates will be enhanced in their efflux behavior while inhibitors will not show enhancement of efflux. This has been shown not only for members of the SLC6-MAT family but also for the GABA transporter GAT1. The authors shall follow these examples to clearly interrogate the substrate status of P4S. With these additional experiments, the already interesting and broad study will be lend support – and be even more powerful.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The manuscript authored by Jing-Xiang Wu and colleagues reports the structures of TauT at a good resolution through cryoEM in complex with taurine, P4S, beta-ala and substrate free states in different conformations. While the study is technically sound, I have the following major concerns that affect the paper’s quality and raises questions that need to be answered. The overall structures of TauT appear to be of a good quality however the authors stop at just reporting the TauT interactions and conformational transitions that are generally in accordance with the other SLC6 members. There seems to be no attempt to study the molecule in depth by making mutations in and around the binding pocket and observing transport kinetics. There seems to be no particularly insightful observations for the mechanism and if there are any characteristics different from other SLC6 members. The conclusions are generally weak and really give no added insight into this transporter group. Further the density of P4S seems to be weak in the occluded state of the transporter. The authors need to give a contoured density separately of P4S. Have any binding sites of P4S observed in the inward-open state of the transporter since the structure in inward open state says that it is P4S inward in fig 1e. A more detailed, direct biochemical evidence is required to ascertain if P4S is indeed a transporter. It cannot be based on structural comparisons. The Authors do not seem to report the presence of any bound detergents or lipids despite achieving a high resolution. In most cases some cholesterol molecules tend to be visible when DDM CHS is used for structure determination. beta-alanine substrate competition and uptake could have been studied to provide more insights into the ability to compete with taurine. This was only done as a qualitative assay whereas a Ki measurement could have been done with beta-alanine. The subsite organization demonstrated here does not highlight altered organization observed in GATs in comparison to the MATs reported earlier. The proper literature for this subsite organization has to be cited as well. Overall the study study reports a set of TauT structures but the conclusions that could have been made through a detailed analyses of substrate recognition and transport mechanisms are lacking. Some more minor comments are given below. - Was the thermal stability assay done using the protein containing GFP-MBP? The higher melting point can be due to the presence of GFP and MBP tags. - Expression construct has no mention of strep tag but in purification, streptactin beads were used for affinity chromatography. - In native PAGE , there is a band which corresponds to MW between 130 to 180 kDa. Could it be some oligomeric species?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The manuscript “Structural mechanism of substrate binding and inhibition of human taurine transporter” describes 6 cryo-EM structures of human taurine transporter (TauT, SLC6A6) bound to taurine, b-alanine, competitive inhibitor P4S, and in substrate-free states. This work is the first presentation of the therapeutically important target, the human TauT structures. While the cryo-EM density maps are of good quality, and the study provides interesting details of the transport cycle, the manuscript can benefit from more in-depth discussion of the findings, placing the study in the context of the wealth of structural and functional data available on SLC6 transporters. Notable issues: - There is no mention of TM5 unwinding and solvation in inward-open states, a characteristic of inward facing states of SLC6 transporters. Whether or not this can be observed, should be discussed. See the reference: Malinauskaite L, et al., doi: 10.1038/nsmb.2894. Epub 2014 Oct 5. PMID: 25282149 - The inward facing states presented in this study, are “inward-open” states, please correct the text accordingly. - Please elaborate on the occluded states, are they outward/inward occluded, or how do they compare to previous SLC6 occluded states, the most similar ones? 249 – 259 discusses this part to some extent but requires further elaboration. - Line 265: ‘and are alternative substrates’, and line 259: ‘This suggests that P4S might be an alternative substrate to hTauT’. This is too definitive based on the evidence presented in the manuscript as to whether P4S is an alternative substrate or substrate analogue. It has only been speculated from structural comparisons, but no functional experiments were carried out. Therefore, it would be best to be more speculative with this statement. - Binding site comparison of taurine-bound TauT with PAT1 (SLC36A1), another taurine transporter, on sequence level (and perhaps on a model basis – alphafold model) could be relevant. - The order of figures does not follow the order they are mentioned in the text, please correct that. - Uptake assay: It is not clear how many replicates were conducted in this assay and what data is being shown (mean? Single data point?). - Is there any indication that P4S gets transported by TauT, whether based on previous studies or experiments performed by the authors? - Local density figure, currently extended data figure 6, should be provided for all the models and maps presented in the manuscript, separately, and not just representative sections of selected models and maps. - Distances should be mentioned for the presented interactions on figures. - Label the TMs on figures, please. - The sigma levels are correctly reported for all the presented density figures; however, it is not clear if they are in reference to Chimera, coot, or? please specify that in the figure legends. - Line 250: The outward-open structure of GlyT1 is not substrate-free! It is bound to competitive inhibitor PF03463275. Models and maps: - There is no density for NAG sites, e.g., in the map 2638, please remove the NAGs from this model and others if the density is not supporting the modelling. - P4S-bound model – occluded state: The fit of the inhibitor could be optimised, the good quality of the density should allow a slightly better fitting. There appears to an interaction of nitrogen group of P4S with CO of E409, if the pose of P4S is modified to fit the density better. If that is the case, the pose should be optimised to see if the interaction is possible. - P4S-bound model – presented as the inward-open It is quite important to clarify whether the P4S also stabilises an inward-open state, or the density in binding pocket accommodates another small molecule. The general fit of the model into density is not finalised, the map is noisy. The noise could originate from the local refinement, if a mask has been used, and needs to be optimised/improved to be evaluated. - Substrate-free states: The substrate-free states can benefit from a section in the manuscript, clearly describing the two states, discussion on differences, if and how they were obtained. They are obtained from one data set, and it’s quite amazing considering the data set is not very large. Please elaborate on the two states, the how, the why, and descriptions in a separate section, similar to other states. In map 2630, there is density around the TM5 region that is not modelled. Could the authors comment on the density whether it is noise (that should be processed better) or if the TM5 can be partially modelled into that density? The map is still noisy, and the model fit at the turns/loop regions can clearly be improved. The disulfide bridge C162-C171 in EL2 seems to be broken in map 2638, please comment on this and other maps. - b-alanine-bound state: There is extra density in the binding pocket. It could nicely accommodate a water molecule and a water mediated interaction of b-alanine with E403. Please consider modelling the Na1 in the b-alanine-bound state, the density is not as strong, but resealable. - Taurine-bound state Extra density in the binding pocket of Taurine-bound state– could be again coordinating water molecule with the Nitrogen of the substrate. Ions binding site – Please add the density to ion binding site figures. Figure 1 – Please present all the models and respective maps at least once in the manuscript.
