peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-to-point response to reviewer comments
We sincerely appreciate the editors and reviewers for their time and insightful
comments. Your valuable and constructive comments are of great importance in
improving our manuscript. As suggested, we have carefully revised our manuscript
and performed additional experiments. We have now completed the revision and
addressed all comments raised by reviewers. Please find the point-to-point responses
below.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Qi, Zhang, and colleagues present human taurine transporter (TauT)
structures in different states, revealing how taurine, β-alanine, and a putative inhibitor
cyclic P4S bind to the substrate-binding site. The authors’ findings provide key insights
into TauT’s transport mechanism, aiding future drug development. The manuscript is
well and clearly written and provides a wealth of data - mostly derived from cryogenic
electron microscopy (cryo-EM) approaches.
Response: We are very grateful to the reviewer for your positive and insightful
comments.
While the structural work is at a very high standard – it does not come along with
biochemical controls as it would be required to support the findings. Just a few things
that the authors may take into consideration exploring:
1) The authors use an N-terminal GFP-MBP tag to use this construct expressed in
HEK293 cells in suspension; however, it has not been described whether the construct
is fully functional. The uptake assay performed in Figure 2, panel A, does not give the
details of whether this particular construct has been used (and there is a typo: wide-
type instead of wild type hTauT). Maybe the authors have performed these
experiments and published the findings in an earlier paper – then, they ought to
simply cite the evidence. If not, they must present the functionality of TauT in this
specific vector by an uptake assay since the assay is anyway already up and running.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the
functionality of our tagged construct. As you suggested, we have compared the
comparative functional characterization between hTauT with the GFP-MBP tag and the
untagged hTauT.
As shown in the new Fig. 2a, we determined the transport kinetics using an LC/MS-
MS-based uptake assay. The tagged hTauT exhibited a Michaelis constant (K ) of 24.8
m
µM, which is highly comparable to the value of 30.5 µM measured for the untagged
construct. Furthermore, after normalization to surface expression levels, the maximal
velocities (V ) were also similar between the two variants (Extended Data Fig. 9a).
max
These new data confirm that the N-terminal GFP-MBP tag does not significantly alter
the key kinetic parameters of hTauT. This finding is consistent with a previously
reported K value of 37.3 µM for a GFP-tagged hTauT construct1. We have
m
incorporated these results and their description into the revised manuscript (Lines 143-
148, Fig. 2a, and Extended Data Fig. 9a).
We also sincerely apologize for the typographical error and have corrected "wide-type"
to "wild-type" in the legend for Figure 2a.
2) The number of structures in occluded or inward-open conformation is impressive
and the authors have made a very good job in deciphering all these. However, since
structural biological answers aided by cryo-EM largely relies on assumptions and
interpretations of data, it would be helpful if the authors would add data of mutagenesis
experiments. The manuscript includes quite a number of very plausible amino acid
contact points with substrates or inhibitors; hence, it would be an easy task to mutate
some key residues to ascertain loss of function and thereby support the findings of the
cryo-EM approach (I am especially focusing on Figure 4 for this request).
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion and for their positive
assessment of our structural work. We fully agree that functional validation is crucial
to corroborate structural observations. In direct response to this comment, we have
performed a comprehensive set of mutagenesis experiments targeting key residues
within the substrate-binding pocket identified in our P4S-bound structure (Fig. 4f).
To systematically validate these interactions, we designed a series of point mutations
targeting residues that coordinate the sulfonate group (e.g., G60, G62, S301), the
hydrophobic subsite (e.g., L306, L134), and the backbone architecture (e.g., G57,).
Surface expression assays confirmed that the majority of these mutants were properly
trafficked to the membrane, with the notable exception of G62Y, which exhibited
reduced expression (Revised Extended Data Fig. 11a).
As the reviewer anticipated, our functional uptake assays provided strong support for
our structural model. Mutations of residues that form direct interactions with both P4S
and the native substrate (e.g., G60Y, L134A, S301A, L306Q) severely impaired or
completely abolished taurine uptake (Fig. 4f). This confirms their essential role in the
binding and transport mechanism.
A particularly insightful result concerns residue E406. Our structure shows that while
E406 forms a critical salt bridge with the amino group of taurine, it does not interact
directly with P4S, whose amino group is positioned differently due to the rigid
piperidine ring. Consistent with this precise structural observation, the E406G mutation
resulted in a complete loss of transport function, underscoring its indispensable role for
substrate binding.
These new mutagenesis data, now incorporated in the revised manuscript (Lines 255-
261, Fig. 4f, and Extended Data Fig. 11a), directly bridge our structural findings with
functional outcomes. They robustly validate the residue-specific interactions we
identified and significantly strengthen the biological conclusions of our study.
3) The question whether cyclic P4S is a substrate or inhibitor cannot be answered by
the assay the group has used in this manuscript. This ought to be done in a trans-
acceleration experiment or also by a release assay: here. tritiated taurine is being
transported into the TauT-expressing cells, and then, unlabeled taurine or unlabeled P4S
is being used in increasing concentrations. In case of taurine, the tritiated taurine will
be released by the transporter upon the inward-transport by the taurine applied from the
outside. However, the problem is that the efflux can be elevated but still not be
decisively showing that the compound is a substrate because in some instances,
pseudo-efflux may take place. Since TauT is a member of the SLC6-family and related to
GABA-transporter, it is dependent on sodium. To determine the substrate status of P4S,
the authors should use monensin, a sodium-proton ionophor, which will selectively
elevate sodium ions intracellularly while depleting protons. This activity will then be
decisive to unravel the substrate status of the compound: Only substrates will be
enhanced in their efflux behavior while inhibitors will not show enhancement of efflux.
This has been shown not only for members of the SLC6-MAT family but also for the
GABA transporter GAT1. The authors shall follow these examples to clearly interrogate
the substrate status of P4S.
With these additional experiments, the already interesting and broad study will be lend
support – and be even more powerful.
Response: We are grateful to the reviewer for this critical suggestion and for providing
the definitive methodological framework to resolve the substrate status of P4S.
Following the reviewer's guidance, we have now performed the decisive monensin-
based efflux assay.
As shown in Revised Fig. 7a, we preloaded HEK293-hTauT cells with [³H]taurine and
measured efflux induced by either unlabeled taurine or P4S. Crucially, pretreatment
with monensin—which selectively elevates intracellular sodium levels—significantly
potentiated the efflux induced by P4S.
This Na⁺-dependent potentiation is a definitive hallmark of a translocated substrate, as
it reports on a Na⁺-coupled exchange process. This result unambiguously distinguishes
a true transported substrate from a static, orthosteric inhibitor, which would not show
enhanced efflux under these conditions2,3. The data therefore provide conclusive
evidence that P4S is not merely a competitive inhibitor but a translocatable substrate
analog that undergoes the full Na⁺-coupled transport cycle.
We have incorporated these findings and their interpretation into the revised manuscript
(lines 371-376, Fig. 7a). This experiment, as the reviewer predicted, has greatly
strengthened our study by providing a powerful functional validation of our structural
observations.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript authored by Jing-Xiang Wu and colleagues reports the structures of
TauT at a good resolution through cryoEM in complex with taurine, P4S, beta-ala and
substrate free states in different conformations. While the study is technically sound, I
have the following major concerns that affect the paper’s quality and raises questions
that need to be answered.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer's thorough assessment and constructive
criticisms, which have significantly strengthened our study.
The overall structures of TauT appear to be of a good quality however the authors stop
at just reporting the TauT interactions and conformational transitions that are generally
in accordance with the other SLC6 members. There seems to be no attempt to study the
molecule in depth by making mutations in and around the binding pocket and observing
transport kinetics. There seems to be no particularly insightful observations for the
mechanism and if there are any characteristics different from other SLC6 members. The
conclusions are generally weak and really give no added insight into this transporter
group.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this critical assessment, which prompted us to
strengthen the mechanistic conclusions of our study. In direct response, we have
performed extensive mutagenesis of the substrate-binding pocket, and this new
functional data—integrated with our structural findings—has revealed key mechanistic
insights that distinguish hTauT from other SLC6 members.
As detailed in our revised manuscript (Fig. 4f, Extended Data Fig. 11a, Lines 255-261),
we designed and characterized a series of point mutations. Surface expression assays
confirmed proper trafficking for most mutants, and functional uptake assays validated
the critical role of residues identified in our structures.
Crucially, this combined approach yielded several novel observations:
Validation of a Divergent Binding Motif: Our structures reveal that hTauT employs
an inverted binding architecture compared to monoamine transporters (e.g., hNET).
In hTauT, the sulfonate group is coordinated in subsite AL by a cluster of backbone amides
and serine/hydroxyl side chains (G60, G62, S301), while the amino group is anchored
in subsite C by a large acidic residue (E406). This is the inverse of the monoamine
transporters, where the amino group is in subsite A and the bulky hydrophobic group
penetrates a larger subsite B. Our mutagenesis confirms that residues defining this
unique motif—including G60, G62, S301, and E406—are absolutely essential for
transport, as the G60Y, G62Y, S301A, and E406G mutants completely abrogate uptake.
Mechanism of Substrate Analog Recognition: The structures of β-alanine-bound and
P4S-bound hTauT provide unique insights into ligand selectivity. For β-alanine, the
subtle but significant reduction in polar interactions for its carboxylate group (with G60
and S402) offers a clear structural rationale for its slightly lower binding affinity
compared to taurine. For P4S, the rigid piperidine ring disrupts the key salt bridge with
E406 that is essential for taurine coordination. These observations provide a direct
structural and mechanistic explanation for the affinities of these ligands, explaining
why β-alanine (Kᵢ = 46.7 μM) and P4S (Kᵢ = 1.4 mM) are lower-affinity substrates or
inhibitors compared to taurine—a nuance not previously understood.
Ligand-Induced Conformational Selection: A major finding of our study is that P4S
binding inverts the intrinsic conformational equilibrium of the transporter. While the
apo state preferentially populates the inward-open conformation (~75%), P4S binding
selectively stabilizes the inward-occluded state (~75%), a phenomenon we directly
demonstrate through particle distribution analysis. This provides a dynamic, energetics-
based view of how a ligand can bias the transport cycle, moving beyond a static
structural description.
In summary, the new mutagenesis data rigorously validate our structural models and
allow us to advance from observation to mechanistic understanding. Our work now
establishes the unique, inverted binding motif of hTauT, explains the structural basis
for substrate analog affinity, and reveals a principle of ligand-induced conformational
selection. We believe these findings provide significant new insight into the SLC6
family by elucidating key structural determinants of substrate specificity and the
dynamic regulation of the transport cycle.
Further the density of P4S seems to be weak in the occluded state of the transporter.
The authors need to give a contoured density separately of P4S. Have any binding sites
of P4S observed in the inward-open state of the transporter since the structure in inward
open state says that it is P4S inward in fig 1e. A more detailed, direct biochemical
evidence is required to ascertain if P4S is indeed a transporter. It cannot be based on
structural comparisons.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these critical and constructive suggestions, which
have been instrumental in strengthening the evidence for our conclusions. We have
addressed these concerns with substantial new experimental data, including improved
structural maps and a definitive functional assay.
Addressing the Density and Map Quality for P4S: We agree that clear ligand density
is paramount. To resolve this, we collected additional cryo-EM data. This effort
improved the resolution of our P4S-bound structures to 2.8 Å (inward-occluded)
and 3.1 Å (inward-open), resulting in clear and unambiguous density for the P4S molecule
in both conformational states (Revised Extended Data Fig. 5). As requested, we now
provide the contoured density for P4S separately in the revised figures (Revised Fig. 4c
and 5b), allowing for direct assessment of its placement.
Confirming P4S Binding in the Inward-Open State: The reviewer correctly inquired
about P4S binding in the inward-open state. Our improved structure confirms that a
well-defined density for P4S is indeed present in the substrate-binding site of the
inward-open conformation, a feature absent in the apo state (Fig. 5b). The ligand's
configuration is nearly identical between the two states. In the inward-open
conformation, the sulfonate group remains engaged with subsite AL, forming hydrogen
bonds with G62 (TM1), Y138 (TM3), S301 (TM6), and S402 (TM8) (Fig. 5c).
The principal conformational change is an ~47° outward splaying of TM1a, which
severs the hydrogen bond with G60 and disrupts the Na1 site, thereby partially
destabilizing P4S interactions (Fig. 5d). This mechanism of ligand retention in a
partially weakened state during a gating transition, which parallels observations in
noradrenaline-bound hNET structures4. These data confirm that P4S remains bound
throughout the conformational cycle.
Providing Direct Biochemical Evidence that P4S is a Transportable Substrate: As
the reviewer rightly emphasizes, structural comparisons alone are insufficient to prove
transportability. Therefore, we performed the decisive monensin-based efflux assay, a
gold-standard functional test for SLC6 transporters. In HEK293-hTauT cells preloaded
with [³H]taurine, P4S induced robust efflux, similar to the native substrate taurine.
Crucially, pretreatment with monensin—which elevates intracellular [Na⁺]—
significantly augmented the P4S-induced efflux (Fig. 7a). This Na⁺-dependent
potentiation is a hallmark of a true transported substrate engaging in exchange transport
and unambiguously distinguishes it from a static inhibitor. Therefore, we conclude with
high confidence that P4S is a translocatable substrate analog, not merely an orthosteric
inhibitor.
These new structural and functional data have been incorporated into the revised
manuscript (Fig. 4c, 5b-d, 7a, and associated text). We believe these additions provide
a conclusive and multi-faceted validation of our model.
The Authors do not seem to report the presence of any bound detergents or lipids despite
achieving a high resolution. In most cases some cholesterol molecules tend to be visible
when DDM CHS is used for structure determination.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion regarding the potential
presence of bound lipids or detergents. In response, we conducted a more detailed
analysis of our cryo-EM maps, particularly following further data collection and
processing that improved the overall resolution, with the β-alanine-bound hTauT
structure now reaching 2.7 Å.
As the reviewer anticipated, the enhanced quality of our maps revealed clear, non-
protein densities at conserved sites known to bind cholesterol or CHS (cholesterol
hemisuccinate) in other SLC6 family transporters. We have successfully modeled these
cholesterol/CHS molecules into their respective densities.
A new panel, Extended Data Fig. 8, has been added to the revised manuscript to
explicitly show the location and density fit of these bound molecules. The
accompanying text in lines 134-141 describes their positions and potential functional
roles, aligning with the established importance of lipid interactions in the stability and
function of SLC6 transporters.
We believe this addition, made possible by our high-resolution structures, provides a
more complete structural description of hTauT and its membrane environment.
beta-alanine substrate competition and uptake could have been studied to provide more
insights into the ability to compete with taurine. This was only done as a qualitative
assay whereas a K measurement could have been done with beta-alanine.
i
Response: We thank the reviewer for this excellent suggestion. In direct response, we
have now quantified the inhibitory effect of β-alanine on hTauT-mediated taurine
uptake.
We performed a dose-response assay, which demonstrates that β-alanine acts as a potent,
dose-dependent competitive inhibitor of taurine uptake (Revised Fig. 3a). The data
yield an IC₅₀ value of 48.96 μM, from which we calculated a Kᵢ value of 46.7 μM. This
measured affinity aligns remarkably well with the previously reported value of 44.5
μM1, thereby validating our experimental approach.
These new quantitative data provide crucial kinetic parameters that strengthen our
structural observations and offer deeper insight into the competitive binding dynamics
between these two substrates at the molecular level. The results have been incorporated
into the revised manuscript (Lines 214-217, Fig. 3a).
The subsite organization demonstrated here does not highlight altered organization
observed in GATs in comparison to the MATs reported earlier. The proper literature for
this subsite organization has to be cited as well.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion regarding the
comparative subsite organization. We have now substantially expanded our analysis to
highlight the distinctive subsite organization of hTauT and related GABA transporters
(GATs) compared to monoamine transporters (MATs), citing the foundational literature
throughout the revised manuscript.
Specifically, we have added a detailed comparative analysis section that explicitly
describes how the substrate-binding architecture in hTauT and GATs represents an
inverted configuration relative to MATs. As noted in the rGAT1 structure, "The primary
binding site of biogenic amine transporters is represented as a group of subsites (A,
B
and C)... In the GAT1 binding site environment, the trilobed binding site is altered to a
bean-shaped binding site with subsites A and C'"5. Similarly, the hGAT1 study observes
that "The substrate binding modes of biogenic amine NSS members such as SERT and
dDAT are quite different from that of GAT1"6.
Our analysis builds upon these foundational observations to demonstrate that hTauT
shares this altered organization with GATs. The key distinction lies in the inversion of
critical residues: in MATs like hNET, a large acidic residue (D75) anchors the
substrate's amino group in subsite A, whereas in hTauT, this position is occupied by a
small glycine (G60) that accommodates the sulfonate group in an enlarged subsite AL.
Conversely, the position occupied by a glycine in MATs contains a large acidic residue
(E406) in hTauT that coordinates the amino group in subsite C.
This comparative analysis, supported by the appropriate citations to hGAT16 and
rGAT15 structures, has been incorporated throughout the revised manuscript (Lines
160-167, Extended Data Fig. 10) and provides crucial context for understanding the
evolutionary adaptation of the SLC6 transporter scaffold.
Overall the study study reports a set of TauT structures but the conclusions that could
have been made through a detailed analyses of substrate recognition and transport
mechanisms are lacking.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this critical assessment, which prompted us to
significantly strengthen the analytical depth and mechanistic conclusions of our study.
We have completely rewritten and expanded the conclusion section to move beyond a
descriptive summary of structures (Lines 394-431). The new text now provides a
synthesized, mechanism-focused narrative that integrates our structural, kinetic, and
mutagenesis data to deliver clear insights into substrate recognition and the transport
cycle.
The core of this new analysis is presented below. It now explicitly:
Articulates a Mechanism for Substrate Specificity: We define the unique, inverted
binding motif of hTauT and explain how specific residues (e.g., the glycine-rich
motif, E406) structurally determine affinity for taurine versus β-alanine and P4S.
Proposes a Dynamic Transport Model: We synthesize observations from multiple
structures into a coherent, stepwise model for intracellular gating and ion/substrate
release, identifying TM1a as the key conformational lever.
Reclassifies a Classic Inhibitor: We use our integrated data to resolve the
mechanism of P4S action, conclusively identifying it as a transported substrate
analog.
We are confident that these substantive additions directly address your concern and
elevate the manuscript's significance by providing the detailed mechanistic analysis
that was previously lacking.
Some more minor comments are given below.
- Was the thermal stability assay done using the protein containing GFP-MBP? The
higher melting point can be due to the presence of GFP and MBP tags.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point regarding the potential
influence of the fusion tags on thermal stability.
The reviewer is correct to highlight this. Our initial thermal stability screening was
conducted using unpurified, GFP-MBP-tagged hTauT in cell lysates via FSEC.
To definitively determine the tag's contribution, we subsequently purified both the GFP-
MBP-tagged and untagged hTauT proteins and performed a quantitative comparison.
The data confirm that the GFP-MBP tag itself confers a significant stabilization, with
the tagged construct exhibiting a melting temperature (T ) of 82 °C, compared to 46 °C
m
for the untagged protein (Extended Data Fig. 1a).
We have incorporated these new data and a clarified description of the methodology
into the revised manuscript (Lines 441-451 and 475-483) to ensure this distinction is
unambiguous for the reader.
- Expression construct has no mention of strep tag but in purification, streptactin beads
were used for affinity chromatography.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their careful attention to this detail. The construct
indeed contains a dual Strep-tag II affinity tag, which was engineered into a solvent-
exposed loop of the GFP moiety. This tag was utilized for affinity purification on
streptactin resin.
We apologize for this omission in the original manuscript and have now explicitly
detailed the presence and location of the Strep-tag in the Methods section (Lines 443-
444) of the revised version.
- In native PAGE, there is a band which corresponds to MW between 130 to 180 kDa.
Could it be some oligomeric species?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question regarding potential
oligomeric species.
The band observed between 130-180 kDa in the original SDS-PAGE (Extended Data
Fig. 1b, middle) corresponds to the monomeric GFP-MBP-hTauT fusion protein, which
has a calculated molecular weight of approximately 144 kDa.
To directly and unequivocally address the question of oligomerization in the native state,
we have now performed native-PAGE analysis on the SEC peak fractions. As shown in
the new Revised Extended Data Fig. 1b, right, the results display a single, dominant
band, confirming the monodisperse nature of the sample and the absence of significant
oligomeric species.
We confirm that these monodisperse fractions were used for cryo-EM grid preparation.
This new data and its interpretation have been incorporated into the revised manuscript
(Lines 88-92 and Revised Extended Data Fig. 1b).
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript “Structural mechanism of substrate binding and inhibition of human
taurine transporter” describes 6 cryo-EM structures of human taurine transporter (TauT,
SLC6A6) bound to taurine, b-alanine, competitive inhibitor P4S, and in substrate-free
states. This work is the first presentation of the therapeutically important target, the
human TauT structures. While the cryo-EM density maps are of good quality, and the
study provides interesting details of the transport cycle, the manuscript can benefit from
more in-depth discussion of the findings, placing the study in the context of the wealth
of structural and functional data available on SLC6 transporters.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their positive feedback and for the detailed
suggestions that have greatly improved the depth and context of our manuscript.
Notable issues:
1. There is no mention of TM5 unwinding and solvation in inward-open states, a
characteristic of inward facing states of SLC6 transporters. Whether or not this can be
observed, should be discussed. See the reference: Malinauskaite L, et al., doi:
10.1038/nsmb.2894. Epub 2014 Oct 5. PMID: 25282149
Response: We thank the reviewer for this critical observation and for directing us to the
foundational reference by Malinauskaite et al. We have now incorporated a detailed
analysis of TM5 conformational changes in our inward-open states as suggested.
Consistent with the characteristic inward-facing state of SLC6 transporters, our
structures of both the apo and P4S-bound hTauT reveal a partially unwound
intracellular segment of TM5 (Revised Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 11b). As
highlighted in the referenced work, this unwinding is a key mechanistic feature that
facilitates the solvation of the intracellular vestibule and the Na2 site, priming the
transporter for substrate and ion release.
A comparative analysis shows that the TM5 conformation in hTauT closely aligns with
the inward-open states of human transporters hGAT1, hGAT3, and hGlyT1, but is
distinct from the outward-tilted TM5 helix observed in the bacterial homolog LeuT
(Revised Extended Data Fig. 11c).
This analysis and the appropriate citation have been incorporated into the revised
manuscript (Lines 264-271) to provide proper mechanistic context for our structural
findings.
2. The inward facing states presented in this study, are “inward-open” states, please
correct the text accordingly.
Response: We thank the reviewer for your suggestions. We have corrected this

3. Please elaborate on the occluded states, are they outward/inward occluded, or how

structural hallmark: the unwinding of the first turn on the intracellular side of TM5 at
the conserved Gly(X9)Pro motif (G243(X9)P253 in hTauT), which leads to hydration
of the Na2 site (Figs. 2b, 3b, 4b). This feature is characteristic of inward-occluded states
in SLC6 transporters, as established in structures of hGAT1 and MhsT (Extended Data
Fig. 9b).
To provide further context, we performed a structural comparison with other SLC6
transporters in similar states. Our analysis confirms that the inward-occluded
conformation of hTauT is most similar to that of GABA-bound hGAT1, with a Cα
RMSD of 1.627 Å (Extended Data Fig. 10a). This quantitative comparison solidifies

landscape of the SLC6 family.

Our new functional data demonstrate that P4S induces efflux of preloaded [³H]taurine
from HEK293-hTauT cells (Revised Fig. 7a). Crucially, pretreatment with monensin -
which elevates intracellular sodium concentration - significantly potentiated this P4S-
induced efflux, mirroring the effect observed with the native substrate taurine (Lines
371-376 and Revised Fig. 7a). This monensin-dependent potentiation is a well-
established characteristic of transported substrates in SLC6 transporters, as it reflects
sodium-coupled exchange2,3.
Based on these comprehensive structural and functional results, we now conclusively
state that P4S acts as a translocated substrate of hTauT, competitively inhibiting taurine
uptake by undergoing the full transport cycle. We have revised the relevant statements
in the manuscript accordingly and included these new data (Fig. 7a and corresponding

5. Binding site comparison of taurine-bound TauT with PAT1 (SLC36A1), another
taurine transporter, on sequence level (and perhaps on a model basis – alphafold model)
could be relevant.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this excellent suggestion. To provide a deeper
evolutionary and mechanistic context, we have performed a detailed comparative
analysis of the substrate-binding sites of hTauT (SLC6A6) and hPAT1 (SLC36A1).
Our analysis, which combines sequence alignment with a structural comparison using
an AlphaFold3-predicted model of hPAT1, reveals a mixed picture of conservation and
divergence. We find that key structural features enabling sulfonate group recognition
are conserved: the small residues that form the enlarged subsite AL in hTauT (G57,
G60, G62, S301) are preserved in hPAT1 (G59, G62, G64, S268). Furthermore, residues
coordinating the substrate's amino group are conservatively substituted (F300 and E406
in hTauT correspond to F267 and Q350 in hPAT1).
However, a critical difference was identified at a position crucial for sodium
coordination. The unique F58 in hTauT, which helps coordinate the Na+ ion at the Na1
site, is not conserved in hPAT1. This divergence in the precise architecture of the
sodium-binding site likely underlies the distinct transport properties of the two
transporters, contributing to hPAT1's characteristically low affinity for taurine (K > 1
m
mM) and broader substrate promiscuity, in contrast to the high-affinity, selective
transport by hTauT.
This new comparative analysis has been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Lines
180-192, Extended Data Fig. 9c, d) and provides valuable insight into how different
transporter families have evolved distinct solutions for recognizing the same substrate.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this important question regarding the transport
status of P4S. Our conclusion that P4S is a transported substrate is supported by
multiple lines of evidence:
First, our structural data demonstrate that P4S binds to both inward-occluded and
inward-open conformations of hTauT, similar to how native substrates like
noradrenaline bind to multiple conformational states in related transporters hNET4.
Structural analysis further confirms that P4S binding is compatible with all major
conformational states in the transport cycle, identical to what we observe for
physiological substrates taurine and β-alanine (Revised Fig. 7b).
Second, previous literature has characterized P4S as both a substrate analog and
competitive inhibitor of hTauT1.
Most definitively, we conducted a decisive monensin-enhanced efflux assay to directly
test the substrate properties of P4S. In HEK293-hTauT cells preloaded with [³H]taurine,
P4S induced efflux comparable to unlabeled taurine. Crucially, monensin pretreatment
- which elevates intracellular sodium concentration - significantly potentiated P4S-
induced efflux, mirroring the effect observed with native taurine. This monensin-
dependent potentiation is a well-established characteristic specific to transported
substrates in SLC6 transporters, as it reflects sodium-coupled exchange kinetics (Lines
371-376 and Fig. 7a).
Therefore, based on comprehensive structural compatibility, previous literature reports,
and definitive functional evidence from the monensin-enhanced efflux assay, we
conclude that P4S acts as a translocatable substrate analog that undergoes the full
transport cycle while competitively inhibiting taurine uptake.

comprehensive description of the substrate-free states, mirroring the detailed analysis

We have elaborated on the methodology in both the Results and Methods sections.
Specifically, we detail how the inward-occluded and inward-open apo states were
resolved from a single cryo-EM dataset. This separation was achieved through
extensive 3D variability analysis (3DVA) and focused 3D classification, which
successfully deconvoluted the pronounced conformational heterogeneity, particularly
within the dynamic TM1a helix. We agree with the reviewer that resolving two distinct
and well-defined conformational states from one dataset is a notable technical outcome
that underscores the dynamic nature of the transporter.
The following paragraph, now included in the manuscript (Lines 92-106), describes this
methodological approach:
“Initial single-particle processing of the apo and P4S-bound datasets indicated
conformational heterogeneity, particularly in the TM1a helix, as evidenced by its
discontinuous and poorly resolved density. This suggested significant flexibility,
contrasting with the well-defined TM1a density observed in the stable, substrate-bound
(taurine/β-alanine) states. To resolve this heterogeneity, we employed 3D variability
analysis (3DVA) in cryoSPARC, which directly visualized the substantial flexibility of
TM1a (Extended Data Movies 1-2). Subsequent focused 3D classification and
refinement successfully separated two distinct conformations from these datasets:
inward-occluded and inward-open (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 5). This strategy enabled
us to determine high-resolution structures of hTauT in multiple conformational states:
the apo state in the inward-occluded conformation and the inward-open conformation
(2.8 Å and 3.1 Å, respectively), the taurine-bound state in the inward-occluded
conformation at 2.9 Å, the β-alanine-bound state in the inward-occluded conformation
at 2.7 Å, and the P4S-bound state in the inward-occluded conformation and inward-
open conformation (2.8 Å and 3.1 Å, respectively) (Extended Data Figs. 2-5 and
Extended Data Table 1).”
Furthermore, in the new dedicated section, we provide a clear description of the two
substrate-free states, their structural features, and the key differences between them.
The section highlights that the transition from the inward-occluded to the inward-open
state is primarily governed by a ~38° outward splaying of TM1a and further unwinding
of TM5, which opens a cytoplasmic pathway. This analysis provides a clear structural
view of the conformational equilibrium in the absence of substrate and directly leads to
our model of a dynamic transporter ensemble.
The core of this new section is presented below (Lines 297-318):
“Following 3DVA and focused 3D classification, we resolved two distinct inward
conformations of apo hTauT (Fig. 1a, b). The inward-occluded conformation,
reconstructed from 149,606 particles, features an occluded substrate-binding site and a
partially unwound intracellular segment of TM5 (Extended Data Fig. 12a). This
conformation is nearly identical to the taurine-bound inward-occluded state, with a
RMSD of 1.250 Å over 550 aligned Cα atoms (Extended Data Fig. 12b). In contrast,
the inward-open conformation, determined from 322,377 particles (~75%), is virtually
superimposable with the P4S-bound inward-open structure (RMSD 0.372 Å; Extended
Data Fig. 11b). A comparison between the two apo conformations reveals that the
transition to the inward-open conformation is characterized by a ~38° outward splaying
of TM1a and further unwinding of the intracellular side of TM5, which opens a
cytoplasmic pathway (Fig. 6a). The predominance of the inward-open conformation in
the apo state indicates that apo hTauT preferentially populates this state. The
coexistence of both conformations suggests the apo transporter samples a dynamic
conformational ensemble, which likely includes outward conformations. We therefore
propose that apo hTauT exists in a dynamic equilibrium; when it transiently visits an
outward-open conformation, taurine binding primes the transporter for translocation.
This intrinsic conformational plasticity is a shared feature among SLC6 transporters,
such as GlyT1 and SERT7,8.
Strikingly, P4S binding inverts this equilibrium. In the P4S-bound state, the majority of
particles (~75%) populate the inward-occluded conformation, with a minority (~25%)
in the inward-open state. This pronounced population shift demonstrates that P4S
binding preferably stabilizes the inward-occluded conformation, which is structurally
rationalized by the enhanced ligand-protein interactions observed in this state (Fig. 5d).”

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-to-point response to reviewer comments
We sincerely appreciate the editors and reviewers for their time and insightful
comments. Your valuable and constructive comments are of great importance in
improving our manuscript. As suggested, we have carefully revised our manuscript
and performed additional experiments. We have now completed the revision and
addressed all comments raised by reviewers. Please find the point-to-point responses
below.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have answered all my questions to full satisfaction.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their positive feedback and are pleased that our
responses and revisions have fully addressed their questions and concerns.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript is significantly improved after the revision and the authors have
answered most of my queries. The study is now quite extensive and adds substantial
information about the mechanisms of substrate selectivity and transport in TauT. A few
minor errors like typos are seen.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their positive assessment of our revised
manuscript and are pleased that they find the study now provides substantial
mechanistic insights into TauT. We are grateful for their constructive feedback
throughout the review process, which has significantly strengthened the work.
In direct response to their final comment, we have conducted a thorough proofreading
of the entire manuscript to identify and correct the minor typographical errors. We are
confident that this final careful edit has further enhanced the clarity and professionalism
of the text.
line 245 - decimal for 2.8 angstroms.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their meticulous proofreading. The typographical
error on line 245 has been corrected from “2.8 angstroms” to “2.8 Å”.
methods: Explain the procedure followed for 3DVA analyses in the methods.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We agree that a detailed
description of the 3DVA procedure will enhance the reproducibility of our work. We
have now added a dedicated paragraph to the Methods section under “Cryo-EM data
processing” to clearly outline the steps and parameters used, as summarized below.
To resolve this heterogeneity, we employed 3D variability analysis (3DVA) in
cryoSPARC. A consensus refinement map, low-pass filtered to 6 Å, served as the initial
reference. A soft mask was applied to focus the analysis on the dynamic TM1a region.
The 3DVA was computed for 3 modes over a maximum of 20 iterations. Following this,
particles were visualized and sorted using the 3DVA display tool in simple mode with
a windowing setting of 2, which organized them into 20 overlapping classes based on
their position along the computed mode. This analysis directly visualized the substantial
flexibility of TM1a (Extended Data Movies 1-2).
Fig. 3a. beta-Alanine Ki curve is not very clean. Needs to be repeated and a cleaner
curve maybe plotted.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their careful evaluation of the binding data. We
acknowledge that the original beta-alanine inhibition curve in Fig. 3a exhibited a degree
of scatter, which reflects the inherent variability of the transport-based functional assay.
In direct response, we repeated the beta-alanine competition experiment in three
additional independent replicates. The newly collected data yield a cleaner sigmoidal
curve and improve confidence in the fitted parameters (Fig. R1). A slight deviation of
one data point (at 5 µM) from the fit is within the expected experimental variability and
does not impact the overall trend or the derived Ki value.
We have now combined all six replicates (original and new) to generate a consolidated,
more robust dataset, which has replaced the original panel in Fig. 3a. This revision
provides a clearer quantitative representation of the inhibition, confirming beta-
alanine's role as a competitive inhibitor of hTauT. We are grateful to the reviewer for
prompting this important validation, which has strengthened our analysis.
Fig. R1 | Inhibition of hTauT by beta-alanine (new data).
Dose–response curve showing beta-alanine inhibition of taurine uptake. Data are
presented as mean ± SEM (n = 3). The curve was fitted to determine an IC of 64.41
50
μM.
besides these aspects I think the manuscript is improved from its earlier version.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have addressed the majority of the points. There are still a few issues that
need correction/clarification. Please revise accordingly.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their continued engagement with our work and
for acknowledging that we have addressed the majority of their points. We are
committed to fully incorporating their remaining feedback to ensure the manuscript
meets the highest standards.
Major Revisions
P4S Inward open structure:
There is unaccounted density near F58. When aligning P4S inward open and P4S
inward occluded, it seems that TM1a from P4S inward occluded could fit here
(particularly F58). Does this mean the particle stack is still mixed and not properly
separated?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation regarding the
unaccounted density near F58 in the P4S-bound inward-open structure, and for raising
the critical question of particle stack homogeneity.
The reviewer's hypothesis is astute. Our initial reconstruction indeed included particles
from both the well-defined cyan class and the lower-resolution yellow class (Fig. R2a).
The yellow class exhibited fragmented TM1a density while retaining some visual
resemblance to an inward-open conformation. This inclusion likely introduced
conformational heterogeneity, manifesting as the ambiguous density near F58.
To address this, we conducted a dedicated re-analysis. Separate 3D reconstructions
revealed a clear distinction: the cyan class displays a continuous TM1a helix, while the
yellow class shows only fragmented density in this region (Fig. R2a). Volume alignment
indicates that the two classes are largely similar except for TM1a. In the yellow class,
TM1a is bent toward the intracellular side and shows a measurable displacement
relative to its position in the cyan class (Fig. R2b). Notably, this displaced TM1a density
more closely resembles that of the inward-occluded conformation (Fig. R2a). Thus, the
yellow class appears to represent an inward-occluded-like, rather than a true inward-
open conformation.
Consequently, for the final refinement, we used only particles from the well-defined
cyan volume, followed by additional 3D classification to remove suboptimal particles.
This stringent processing yielded a homogeneous particle set and a final map at ~3.25
Å resolution. Crucially, in this revised map, the density near F58 is well-resolved and
clear (Fig. R2c). The minimal, discontinuous residual density that cannot accommodate
the TM1a helix from the inward-occluded conformation, confirming that the initial
prominent unaccounted density was an artifact of the previously mixed particle set.
Thus, the final structure represents a well-separated, homogeneous conformation. We
have updated Extended Data Fig. 5 and its legend.
The updated cryo-EM map and model for the P4S-bound inward-open conformation
have been deposited in EMDB and PDB under the same accession codes.
Fig. R2 | Revised cryo-EM analysis of the P4S-bound hTauT inward-open
conformation.
a. Focused 3D classification workflow. The cryo-EM density for TM1a is continuous
in the cyan class but fragmented in the yellow class. The black box indicates volume
alignment between the yellow class and the P4S-bound inward-occluded conformation
(light blue; map contoured at 12.2 σ). The position of TM1a in the yellow volume (black
circle) resembles that of the inward-occluded state.
b. Overall map alignment of the cyan and yellow classes. The arrow indicates the
displacement of TM1a density between the two classes (maps contoured at 12.2 σ).
c. Comparison of the revised (blue mesh, left) and previous (yellow mesh, right) cryo-
EM maps of the P4S-bound inward-open conformation, displayed in Coot at two
contour levels. Structural models of the P4S-bound inward-open (green) and inward-
occluded (split-pea) conformations are fitted to the density near F58. Red arrows
indicate that the improved density in the revised map (contoured at 7.0 σ) cannot
accommodate TM1a from the inward-occluded conformation.
In this model, the density of CHS703 does not support modelling of the CHS molecule,
please remove it.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their careful scrutiny of the structural model. We
have re-examined the revised electron density map for CHS703 and agree that the
density is insufficient to confidently model this molecule. Accordingly, we have
removed CHS703 from the model to ensure it accurately reflects the experimental data.
Apo inward open
There is density that matches where P4S was modelled in the inward open structure (it
only disappears at 10 rmsd in Coot). This raises questions about the confidence of P4S
in the inward open structure. What could this density represent in the substrate-free map?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this exceptionally perceptive question regarding
the residual density in the substrate-free, inward-open map. We agree that its
interpretation is crucial.
Our initial reconstruction of the apo inward-open conformation included particles from
both the cyan and yellow 3D classes. As detailed in our response concerning Extended
Data Fig. 2c, the yellow class exhibits poorly defined TM1a density and likely
introduced conformational heterogeneity, which may account for the ambiguous
density noted by the reviewer.
Following the reviewer’s comment, we performed a detailed re-analysis. The final,
refined apo inward-open structure presented in the manuscript was obtained using only
particles from the well-defined cyan volume, following additional 3D classification to
ensure homogeneity. This more stringent particle selection yielded a map in which the
central binding site is unambiguous and shows no significant unmodeled density
corresponding to the P4S position (even at a contour level as low as 7.8 σ in Coot; Fig.
R3), despite a modest reduction in resolution (from ~3.18 Å to ~3.33 Å).
Therefore, we conclude that the residual density in the earlier reconstruction was an
artifact of the initial, mixed particle set. Its absence in the final, rigorously processed
map reinforces both the conformational purity of the apo inward-open state and the high
confidence in the modeled P4S ligand within the P4S-bound structure.
Fig. R3 | Ligand-binding site density in the inward-open conformation.
a. Cryo-EM density (gray mesh, contoured at 7.8 σ) for P4S and surrounding residues
(green) in the P4S-bound inward-open structure (left), compared with the
corresponding region in the apo inward-open state (right, empty density), displayed in
ChimeraX.
b. Equivalent view displayed in Coot, showing the revised density (blue mesh) for the
P4S-bound state (green model) and the empty density (light pink mesh) for the apo state
(brown model), both contoured at 7.8 σ.
In the inward occluded apo structure, the two water molecules have been modelled into
the density (but it is clearer density there).
Response: We thank the reviewer for their careful scrutiny of the structural model. As
noted in our response regarding Extended Data Fig. 2c, we have reprocessed the data
for the apo inward-occluded state. The regenerated electron density map shows no clear
density at the previously modeled water sites. Consequently, water molecules have been
omitted from these positions in the final model to ensure it accurately reflects the
experimental data.
The density for CLR702 does not support modelling of the CLR molecule, please
remove it.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their careful scrutiny of the structural model. Upon
re-examining the revised electron density map, we agree that the density for CLR702
is insufficient to support its modeling.
As detailed in our response regarding Extended Data Fig. 2c, the final reconstruction
of the apo inward‑occluded state used only particles from the well‑separated cyan
volume, which led to a modest reduction in nominal resolution (from ∼3.18 Å to
∼3.33 Å). In this refined map, the density for CHS703 is also inadequate for reliable
modeling due to the lower overall resolution. Consequently, CHS703 has also been
omitted from the final model.
These adjustments ensure that the atomic model accurately reflects the experimental
density.
Water801 is modelled in 9L1B but density here is only visible at the level of the noise.
Please remove it from the model.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their meticulous attention to the structural model.
We agree with this observation. Upon re-examining the electron density map for the
9L1B structure, we confirm that the density for Water801 is indeed weak and does not
meet the threshold for reliable modeling. In accordance with standard structural
refinement practices, Water801 has been omitted from the revised model.
Whilst the monensin experiments provide compelling evidence that P4S is a substrate,
it is still an indirect measure of P4S transport. I would therefore temper the language of
line 305 “definitive hallmark”
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that the
monensin-based assay, while a powerful and established functional tool, provides
indirect evidence of transport. Accordingly, we have tempered the language in the
revised manuscript (line 375).
The phrase "a definitive hallmark" has been replaced with "a key functional
characteristic consistent with SLC6 substrate translocation".
This revision more accurately reflects the inferential nature of the evidence while still
underscoring the significance of the observed Na+-dependent, substrate-stimulated
ionophore activity. This change strengthens our manuscript by presenting a more
precise interpretation that is fully aligned with the experimental data. We believe this
adjustment addresses the reviewer's valid concern effectively.
In Extended Fig. 2c, it is not clear why particles of the yellow volume were included,
please elaborate (close up screenshot is attached).
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this point regarding Extended Data Fig.
2c, which allows us to clarify our particle selection strategy.
The yellow volume, though exhibiting poor density for TM1a, showed some visual
resemblance to an inward-open conformation (Fig. R4a). To avoid discarding particles
that might belong to the inward-open conformation, we initially retained this entire
class for further analysis.
Following the reviewer’s comment, we performed a detailed re-analysis. Separate 3D
reconstructions revealed a clear difference: the cyan class shows a continuous TM1a
helix, whereas the yellow class displays only fragmented density in this region (Fig.
R4a). Volume alignment shows that the two classes are largely similar except for TM1a.
In the yellow class, TM1a is bent toward the intracellular side and shows a measurable
displacement relative to its position in the cyan class (Fig. R4b). Notably, this displaced
TM1a density more closely resembles that of the inward-occluded conformation (Fig.
R4a).
These results demonstrate that the yellow class does not represent a homogeneous
inward-open state, but rather a heterogeneous ensemble in which TM1a samples a
position intermediate toward—or akin to—the inward-occluded conformation.
Consequently, in the final processing workflow, we used only particles from the well-
defined cyan volume for high-resolution refinement, followed by additional 3D
classification to remove suboptimal particles.
We have updated Extended Data Fig. 2c and its legend. Furthermore, this refined
processing yielded a revised map for the inward-open apo state in which density at the
canonical chloride-binding site is absent. Given the lack of supportive density—
potentially due to the lower resolution or chloride release in this state—we have
removed the modeled chloride from the final atomic model. The related figures
(Revised Figs. 6g and 7g) have been updated with the revised maps and models.
The updated cryo-EM map and model for the P4S-bound inward-open conformation
have been deposited in EMDB and PDB under the same accession codes.
Fig. R4 | Analysis of conformational heterogeneity in apo inward-open hTauT.
a. Focused 3D classification workflow. The cryo-EM density for TM1a is continuous
in the cyan class but fragmented in the yellow class. The black box indicates volume
alignment between the yellow class and the apo inward-occluded conformation (light
orange; maps contoured at 11.9 σ). The position of TM1a in the yellow volume (black
circle) resembles that of the inward-occluded state.
b. Overall map alignment of the cyan and yellow classes (contoured at 11.9 σ). The
arrow highlights the displacement of TM1a density between the two classes.
Line 205: remove (ref)
Response: We thank the reviewer for catching this oversight. The placeholder "(ref)"
on line 205 has been removed as requested.
Line 242: In light of the new results presented in the manuscript showing P4S is a
substrate, specifying that “P4S acts as a competitive inhibitor of taurine transport by
hTauT” may be more appropriate
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion.
We have revised the text on line 242 as recommended. This change more precisely
describes P4S's mechanism of action and better integrates the structural findings with
their functional context. We are grateful to the reviewer for this valuable clarification.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Taurine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that plays several crucial roles in the body. Its uptake is mediated by the taurine transporter (TauT). Genetic mutations and dysregulation of TauT have been linked to various neurological disorders, cardiomyopathy, childhood progressive retinal degeneration, and cancer, making TauT a promising target for therapeutic intervention in these diseases. However, the structure and mechanism of TauT remain poorly understood. In this study, we present the structures of the human taurine transporter (hTauT) under four conditions: the substrate-free state, the taurine-bound state, the β-alanine-bound state, and the cyclic inhibitor piperidine-4-sulfonate (P4S)-bound state. These structures reveal that taurine binds at the central substrate-binding site of hTauT. Notably, β-alanine and the cyclic P4S inhibitors also mimic taurine, occupying the same substrate-binding site. In the substrate-free and P4S-bound forms, hTauT also adopt an inward-open conformation, where transmembrane helix TM1a bends toward the membrane, facilitating the opening of the intracellular gate for ion and substrate release. These structural insights enhance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying substrate and ion recognition and transport in hTauT, paving the way for the future development of taurine transporter substrate analogues or selective inhibitors.

---

## Introduction

Taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonic acid) is an abundant nonprotein β-amino acid and a conditionally essential nutrient widely distributed in most tissues of humans. Taurine has various physiological functions, including energy metabolism, osmoregulation, antioxidation, and neuromodulation 1. Taurine deficiency causes functional impairments in the central nervous system, cardiovascular system, immune response, skeletal muscle, and eye 1-5. The intracellular high levels of taurine are mainly regulated by the taurine transporters (TauT), which take taurine into cells 6. TauT-knockout mice exhibit aging characteristics, such as exercise intolerance and muscle atrophy, retinal and inner ear degeneration, renal development and function alteration, and cardiomyopathy 7,8. Mutations in the TauT genes are associated with neurological disorders, cardiomyopathy, and childhood progressive retinal degeneration in humans 9. In addition, TauT is overexpressed in several malignancies, such as colorectal (CRC), gastric (GC), and cervical cancers (CC), causing poor prognosis, immune evasion, aggressive and invasive progression, and recurrence of tumors 10-12. Therefore, TauT could be a promising diagnostic imaging and therapy target 13,14.

TauT (also known as SLC6A6) is a member of the solute carrier 6 (SLC6) family, which is divided into four subfamilies according to their substrate similarity—GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid), monoamine, neurotransmitter amino acid, and nutrient amino acid transporters. TauT shares >36% sequence similarity with other SLC6 family members, and has the highest sequence identity with GAT3 (~61%) 15. TauT, along with GAT1 (SLC6A1), GAT2 (SLC6A13), GAT3 (SLC6A11), BGT1 (SLC6A12), and CT1 (SLC6A8), belong to the GABA transporter subfamily 13. SLC6s can utilize the chemiosmotic gradient of sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl-) ions to transport their substrates across the membrane 15. For TauT, substrate uptake occurs with a stoichiometry of 2 Na⁺:1 Cl⁻. Today, the substrate taurine of TauT has been approved for treating congestive heart failure 1. Taurine also shows potential in acting as a therapeutic agent to treat muscle diseases 16, neurological disorders 17,18, cardiovascular diseases 19, metabolic diseases 18, and cancer 20. Inhibition of TauT could be a promising strategy in cancer treatment, yet only limited inhibitors that are structurally similar to substrate have been investigated. β-alanine is a linear inhibitor of TauT, previously identified as the substrate of TauT to take up with high efficiency in neuronal and astroglial cells 21,22. Piperidine-4-sulfonate (P4S) is a cyclic inhibitor of TauT developed with the amine group incorporated into the ring 23. P4S shows a relatively higher affinity than other investigated inhibitors and provides a potential lead structure to design specific drug candidates of TauT for therapy of cancer and neurodegenerative diseases 23.

Understanding how substrate binds to and is transported by TauT and inhibitors act on TauT are critical questions in the field of TauT. The taurine binding site on TauT was mapped based on the structure of Aquifex aeolicus LeuT, and mutations of several residues have been shown to significantly influence substrate recognition and uptake function of TauT 24. Moreover, homology modelling of TauT based on the related subfamily member GAT1 structure has provided valuable insights into the protein-ligand interactions 13. However, the structure of TauT remains unknown, precluding a thorough understanding of its transport mechanism and the structure-based development of medications.

Here, we show cryo-EM structures of human TauT (hTauT) in the apo, taurine-bound, β-alanine-bound, and P4S-bound states in the inward-occluded conformation at resolutions ranging from 2.7 to 2.9 Å, respectively. The apo state and the P4S-bound state also show inward-open conformations. These structures reveal the overall architecture, the linear substrate- and ion-binding sites, the conformational transition of hTauT, as well as the inhibitory mechanism of the cyclic P4S.
